1.lecture:
§1 · Design is analysis run backwards

Analysis asks: given this part, what stress appears? Design asks the harder inverse: given this load and this consequence of failure, what part? Analysis has one answer; design has a family of them, and the engineering is in the choosing. Every design decision is therefore two decisions — a size, and a reason for that size that survives being questioned a year later by someone holding a broken piece of it.

§2 · Load cases before geometry

The first discipline is refusing to size anything until the load cases are written down. Steady operating load is rarely the governing one. Start-up torque, upset pressure, thermal growth against a fixed anchor, a dropped tool, a lifting case during maintenance, and the seismic or wind case if the structure is outdoors — each is a separate load case, and the part must survive the worst of them, not their average. A part that fails in service almost never failed under the load the designer analysed; it failed under the one nobody wrote down.

§3 · The factor of safety, honestly

The factor of safety is the ratio of the strength you rely on to the stress you expect:

Key relation — design margin

\[ n = \frac{S}{\sigma}, \qquad \sigma_{allow} = \frac{S}{n} \]

\( S \) is the governing strength — yield for permanent-deformation limits, ultimate for rupture, endurance limit for fatigue — and \( \sigma \) is the stress the load case produces. Choosing \( n \) is choosing how much ignorance you are buying insurance against.

What \( n \) actually covers is worth naming, because it is not one thing: scatter in material properties, uncertainty in the load, idealisation error in the analysis, degradation in service, and the consequence of failure. A bracket holding a cable tray and a bracket holding a pressure vessel get different numbers for the last reason alone. A large \( n \) is not conservatism; it is an admission of how much you do not know, and it is expensive in mass, cost and — in rotating equipment — in the very inertia you are trying to control.

§4 · The design working method

Use the same sequence every time. One: write the load cases, each with its source and its own worst-credible magnitude. Two: identify the failure mode each case could provoke — yielding, rupture, fatigue, buckling, wear, leakage — because the governing strength depends on the mode, not on the load. Three: choose \( n \) and record why, in the calculation, in one sentence. Four: size the part, then check every other failure mode against that size; the mode that governs is rarely the one you started with. Five: state the result as a drawing callout, not as a stress — a number that cannot be inspected has not been designed.

Codes and standards are encoded experience, and they deserve respect precisely because they are other people's failures written down. But a code gives a floor, not an answer: it tells you the minimum a competent engineer may claim, and it assumes you have identified the right load cases and the right failure mode. Meeting a code with the wrong load case is fully compliant and fully wrong.

Closing. Design is a defensible size. The margin is yours to justify, the load cases are yours to enumerate, and the code is a floor beneath both.

  • Axial stress and strain (Strength of Materials L1) — \( \sigma = F/A \) and what yield means physically.
  • Material property vocabulary (Materials I L7) — yield strength, tensile strength, ductility, and which is a design stress.
  • Free-body diagrams (Statics L3) — every load case begins as one.

quiz.q:
Sizing to an allowable, not to a stress

Problem. A tension link carries a steady load \( F = 12\ \mathrm{kN} \). The material has a yield strength \( S_y = 250\ \mathrm{MPa} \). The proposed section area is \( 300\ \mathrm{mm^2} \). Find: the working stress, the resulting factor of safety against yield, and the allowable stress if the design standard requires \( n = 2 \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Working stress: \( \sigma = F/A = 12\,000/300\times10^{-6} = 40\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) Factor of safety on yield: \( n = S_y/\sigma = 250/40 = 6.25 \). (3) Allowable at the required \( n = 2 \): \( \sigma_{allow} = 250/2 = 125\ \mathrm{MPa} \).

Answer: 40 MPa working, \( n = 6.25 \), allowable 125 MPa. Sanity check: the working stress sits well under the allowable, so the link passes with room to spare — which is itself a finding. A part running at \( n = 6.25 \) where the standard asks for 2 is carrying mass and cost nobody specified, and is worth a second look before it is multiplied across a hundred assemblies.

quiz.q:
What the margin buys you

Problem. The same link, sized as above, is found in service to carry 20% more load than the design case because an upstream damper was removed. Find: the new working stress and factor of safety, and state whether the part is still acceptable against a required \( n = 2 \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) New load: \( 1.2 \times 12 = 14.4\ \mathrm{kN} \), so \( \sigma = 14\,400/300\times10^{-6} = 48\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) \( n = 250/48 = 5.21 \). (3) Required is \( n = 2 \); actual is 5.21, so the link remains acceptable.

Answer: 48 MPa, \( n = 5.21 \), still acceptable. Sanity check: this is exactly what margin is for — an unlisted load case appeared and the part absorbed it. Note what the calculation does not say: it does not say removing the damper was harmless. Fatigue and the components downstream were never checked, and a 20% load rise is a far larger rise in fatigue damage, as Lessons 3 and 4 will show.

quiz.q:
Choosing n with a reason attached

Problem. Two brackets use the same material and see the same 40 MPa working stress. Bracket A supports a lighting conduit in an accessible corridor. Bracket B supports a pipe carrying hot process fluid above a walkway. Find: a defensible factor of safety for each and the resulting allowable stresses, and state the single dominant reason they differ.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The stress analysis is identical, so nothing in the mechanics distinguishes them. (2) The consequence of failure does not: A drops a conduit in a place where people can see and reach it; B releases hot fluid over a walkway, where failure injures people. (3) A defensible pair is \( n_A = 2 \) giving \( \sigma_{allow} = 125\ \mathrm{MPa} \), and \( n_B = 4 \) giving \( \sigma_{allow} = 62.5\ \mathrm{MPa} \) — B is then sized to roughly twice the area for the same load.

Answer: \( n_A \approx 2 \), \( n_B \approx 4 \); the dominant reason is consequence of failure, not uncertainty in load or material. Sanity check: the exact numbers are a judgement and a standard may set them for you. What is not a judgement is that they must differ, and that the reason is recorded. An engineer who sizes both at \( n = 2 \) has not made an error of arithmetic; they have made an error of scope.

quiz.q: A component is sized against yield with \( S_y = 250\ \mathrm{MPa} \) and a required factor of safety \( n = 2.5 \). What is the allowable stress?
choices: \( 100\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 625\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 252.5\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 247.5\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
quiz.solution: The allowable stress is the strength divided by the factor of safety: \( \sigma_{allow} = S_y/n = 250/2.5 = 100\ \mathrm{MPa} \). The 625 MPa answer multiplies instead of divides, which would license a stress above yield — the direction of the error is the giveaway, since a factor of safety must always reduce what you may claim. The 252.5 and 247.5 answers treat the factor as something to add to or subtract from the strength; a factor of safety is a ratio, and it is dimensionless precisely so that it scales rather than offsets.

quiz.q: A pressure-retaining part is designed strictly to the minimum a code permits, using the load cases the designer listed. In service it fails. Which statement best describes the situation?
choices: The code is invalid and should not have been used
Code compliance is a floor, and it assumes the right load cases and failure mode were identified
The factor of safety must have been below 1.0
Codes apply only to materials, not to load cases
quiz.solution: A code encodes other people's failures and sets the minimum a competent engineer may claim. It cannot know which load cases exist in your plant. Meeting a code against an incomplete list of load cases is fully compliant and still wrong, which is why enumerating load cases precedes sizing in the working method. The factor of safety was almost certainly above 1.0 for the case analysed — that is the point: the governing case was not analysed. Codes plainly do address loading and failure modes, not just materials.

quiz.q: Which of the following is not one of the uncertainties a factor of safety is intended to cover?
choices: Scatter in material properties
Uncertainty in the applied load
An arithmetic mistake in the stress calculation
Degradation of the part in service
quiz.solution: The factor of safety covers scatter in properties, uncertainty in load, idealisation error in the model, service degradation, and the consequence of failure. It is not an allowance for arithmetic errors, and treating it as one is dangerous: a wrong calculation can be wrong by any factor at all, including orders of magnitude, whereas the margin is sized for bounded, anticipated variation. Arithmetic is controlled by checking, not by margin.

quiz.q: A part is sized for its steady operating load. Which of these is most likely to be the load case that actually governs its size?
choices: The steady operating load, since it acts for the longest time
The average of all load cases
A short-duration start-up or upset case
Whichever case produces the lowest stress
quiz.solution: Steady operating load is rarely governing precisely because everything is comfortable there. Start-up torque, upset pressure, thermal growth against an anchor and maintenance lifting cases are short but large, and a part must survive the worst credible case, not the average or the most frequent one. Duration matters for fatigue and creep, not for a yield check. Sizing to the lowest-stress case inverts the entire exercise.

quiz.q: Reported as a margin of safety, a component with a factor of safety \( n = 1.35 \) has \( MS \) equal to
quiz.solution: Margin of safety is defined as \( MS = n - 1 \), so \( 1.35 - 1 = 0.35 \); a non-negative value means the case is satisfied, and the convention exists so that "zero" reads as "exactly adequate" rather than "no strength". Reporting 1.35 confuses the margin with the factor itself. The 0.74 answer is \( 1/1.35 \), the stress-to-strength ratio, which is a utilisation rather than a margin.

quiz.q: Two designers size the same bracket. One reports "the stress is 40 MPa". The other reports "6 mm plate, 50 mm wide, per drawing callout". Which has completed a design?
choices: The first, because the stress is the engineering result
The second, because a size that can be inspected is the deliverable
Both equally
Neither, without a fatigue check
quiz.solution: Analysis returns a stress; design returns a size, and a size that cannot be inspected has not been designed. The drawing callout is the deliverable because it is what the shop builds and what the inspector measures against. The first report is a necessary intermediate, not an output. A fatigue check may well be required, but its absence does not turn the second report into a non-design — it identifies a further load case to assess, which is exactly the working method's step four.

quiz.q: Increasing a factor of safety from 2 to 4 on a tension member, for the same load and material, has what effect on the required cross-sectional area?
choices: Halves it
Doubles it
Leaves it unchanged
Quadruples it
quiz.solution: For a tension member \( A = F n / S \), so the area is directly proportional to \( n \): doubling the factor doubles the area, and with it the mass and the material cost. Halving is the same relation read backwards. It is unchanged only if the factor plays no part in sizing, which would make it decorative. Quadrupling would require an area proportional to \( n^2 \), which holds for neither axial nor bending sizing — in bending the section modulus scales with \( n \), so the depth grows more slowly still.

quiz.q: Which strength should govern the factor of safety for a part whose failure criterion is "must not deform permanently"?
choices: Ultimate tensile strength
Yield strength
Endurance limit
Hardness
quiz.solution: Permanent deformation is yielding, so the yield strength governs. Ultimate tensile strength describes rupture and would permit the part to deform grossly while remaining "safe" against the wrong criterion. The endurance limit governs fatigue under fluctuating load, a different failure mode. Hardness is a proxy for strength, useful for field triage, but it is not itself a design strength — a point Materials I made when it warned that hardness correlations are empirical.

1.kuwait: Applied case — the bracket that passed and the bracket that mattered. During a plant modification, a contractor supplies two identical brackets from the same drawing: one supports an instrument-air line, the other a small steam header above a maintenance walkway. The calculation package sizes both at \( n = 2 \) against yield, and the arithmetic is correct in both. A design review rejects the package — not for its stress analysis, which is sound, but for its scope: the two brackets have the same mechanics and different consequences, and the calculation never says so. The steam bracket is re-sized at \( n = 4 \) and, more importantly, the calculation now carries one sentence explaining why. The reviewer's objection was not conservatism; it was that a margin without a stated reason cannot be checked, revised, or defended when the plant changes around it.
1.recap:
• Analysis asks what stress a given part sees; design asks the inverse — given the load and the consequence of failure, what part? Analysis has one answer, design has a family.
  • Write the load cases before sizing anything: start-up, upset, thermal growth against a fixed anchor, dropped tool, maintenance lifting, wind or seismic. The part must survive the worst, not the average.
  • Parts that fail in service rarely failed under the load that was analysed — they failed under the one nobody wrote down.
  • The design margin is \( n = S/\sigma \), with \( S \) the strength governing the failure mode: yield for permanent set, ultimate for rupture, endurance limit for fatigue.
  • \( n \) covers several distinct things — material scatter, load uncertainty, idealisation error, service degradation, and the consequence of failure. A cable-tray bracket and a pressure-vessel bracket differ on the last alone.
  • A large \( n \) is not conservatism but an admission of ignorance, and it costs mass, money and — on rotating equipment — the inertia the design is trying to control.
  • Work the same sequence every time: load cases, failure modes, choose and record \( n \), size, then re-check every other mode against that size — the governing mode is rarely the one you started with.
  • Codes and standards are encoded experience: they carry the failures that shaped them, which is why departing from one requires an argument rather than a preference.

2.lecture:
§1 · One number from a stress state

Material strength is quoted from a tension test — a single axis, a single number. Real parts carry combined stress: bending with torsion, pressure with axial load, a bolt in tension while a joint shears. A failure theory is the bridge, collapsing a multiaxial stress state into one equivalent stress that may be compared against the tensile yield strength honestly.

§2 · Von Mises and Tresca

Key relations — the two static theories

\[ \sigma' = \sqrt{\sigma_x^2 - \sigma_x\sigma_y + \sigma_y^2 + 3\tau_{xy}^2}, \qquad \sigma_{Tresca} = \sigma_{max} - \sigma_{min} \]

Von Mises (distortion energy) predicts yielding of ductile metals most accurately; Tresca (maximum shear) is always the more conservative of the two, by up to about 15%.

Both take the same input and answer the same question, and Tresca never predicts a higher capacity than von Mises. That is why codes fond of conservatism adopt Tresca while a designer chasing mass adopts von Mises — and why quoting a factor of safety without naming the theory is an incomplete statement.

§3 · Stress concentrations, counted honestly

Nominal stress is what the average section carries; a hole, a fillet or a keyway multiplies it locally by a geometric factor \( K_t \), so \( \sigma_{max} = K_t \sigma_{nom} \). For a static load on a ductile material, local yielding blunts the peak and redistributes it, so \( K_t \) is commonly set aside. Under fatigue, or in a brittle material, that permission is withdrawn entirely — which is the bridge to Lesson 3, and the reason a shaft's shoulder radius is a design variable rather than a drafting convenience.

§4 · The static sizing method

One: resolve the stress state at the worst point — usually a surface, usually at a discontinuity. Two: get the principal stresses, by Mohr's circle or by formula. Three: pick a theory and say which. Four: compare against \( S_y/n \). Five: decide whether \( K_t \) applies — ductile and static, usually not; brittle or fatigue, always. The commonest error in practice is comparing a raw shear stress against a tensile yield strength, which mixes two incompatible quantities and is optimistic by roughly the factor \( \sqrt{3} \).

Closing. A failure theory is a translator, not a truth. Name the one you used, and the number you report becomes checkable.
2.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Principal stresses and Mohr's circle (Strength of Materials) — the transformation itself, not just the formula.
  • Yield strength (Materials I L7) — a tensile-test number being borrowed for a multiaxial state.
  • Factor of safety (Lesson 1) — the allowable stress this lesson compares against.

Glossary

TermEquationWhen to use
Von Mises stress\( \sigma' = \sqrt{\sigma_x^2-\sigma_x\sigma_y+\sigma_y^2+3\tau_{xy}^2} \)Ductile metals under static combined stress; the accurate default.
Tresca stress\( \sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min} \)When the code or the consequence calls for the conservative theory.
Principal stresses\( \tfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2}\pm\sqrt{(\tfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2})^2+\tau_{xy}^2} \)The input both theories need; remember the third principal is zero in plane stress.
Stress concentration\( \sigma_{max}=K_t\sigma_{nom} \)Holes, fillets, keyways; mandatory under fatigue or in brittle material.
Pure shear equivalence\( S_{sy}\approx 0.577\,S_y \)Shear yield from tensile yield, via von Mises.

quiz.q:
The same state, two theories

Problem. A shaft surface carries \( \sigma_x = 80\ \mathrm{MPa} \) bending and \( \tau_{xy} = 40\ \mathrm{MPa} \) torsional shear, with \( \sigma_y = 0 \). \( S_y = 250\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Find: the principal stresses, the von Mises and Tresca equivalent stresses, and the factor of safety by each theory.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Centre \( (80+0)/2 = 40 \); radius \( \sqrt{40^2+40^2} = 56.57\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Principals: \( 96.57 \) and \( -16.57\ \mathrm{MPa} \), with the third equal to zero. (2) Von Mises: \( \sqrt{80^2 + 3(40)^2} = \sqrt{11\,200} = 105.83\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (3) Tresca: \( \sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min} = 96.57-(-16.57) = 113.14\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (4) \( n_{VM} = 250/105.83 = 2.36 \); \( n_{T} = 250/113.14 = 2.21 \).

Answer: 96.6 / −16.6 MPa; \( \sigma' = 105.8 \), \( \sigma_{Tresca} = 113.1 \) MPa; \( n = 2.36 \) or \( 2.21 \). Sanity check: Tresca is 6.9% higher in stress and correspondingly lower in factor of safety, inside the expected 0–15% band. If your two theories ever disagree by more than about 15%, the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics.

quiz.q:
When the concentration counts

Problem. A ductile steel plate with \( S_y = 250\ \mathrm{MPa} \) carries a nominal tensile stress of 40 MPa through a section containing a hole with \( K_t = 2.5 \). Find: the peak local stress, and state whether the part yields (a) under a static load and (b) if the same plate were a brittle casting.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Peak: \( \sigma_{max} = K_t\sigma_{nom} = 2.5\times40 = 100\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) Static, ductile: 100 MPa is below \( S_y = 250 \), so no yielding; and even had it exceeded yield locally, the ductile material would redistribute rather than fracture. (3) Brittle casting: no redistribution is available, so the 100 MPa peak is the stress that must be compared against the material's (much lower) tensile capacity, and \( K_t \) cannot be set aside.

Answer: 100 MPa peak; safe statically in ductile steel; \( K_t \) governs in a brittle casting. Sanity check: the difference is not in the stress — it is 100 MPa in both — but in whether the material can shed the peak. That single distinction is why cast housings crack at fillets that would be unremarkable in a forging.

quiz.q:
Shear yield is not tensile yield

Problem. A pin is loaded in pure shear. The material has \( S_y = 250\ \mathrm{MPa} \) in tension. Find: the shear yield strength by the von Mises criterion, and the factor of safety if the pin carries \( 80\ \mathrm{MPa} \) of shear.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) For pure shear, \( \sigma_x=\sigma_y=0 \), so \( \sigma' = \sqrt{3}\,\tau \). Yielding begins when \( \sqrt{3}\,\tau = S_y \), giving \( S_{sy} = S_y/\sqrt{3} = 0.577\times250 = 144.3\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) \( n = 144.3/80 = 1.80 \).

Answer: \( S_{sy} = 144.3\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( n = 1.80 \). Sanity check: comparing the 80 MPa shear directly against the 250 MPa tensile yield would have reported \( n = 3.13 \) — optimistic by exactly \( \sqrt{3} \), and the single most common static-design error in the field. A pin "with a factor of three" can in fact be sitting at 1.8.

quiz.q: For the same stress state, which statement about the two static failure theories is always true for a ductile metal?
choices: Von Mises predicts a lower equivalent stress than Tresca
Tresca predicts a lower equivalent stress than von Mises
They always agree exactly
Which is lower depends on the material
quiz.solution: Tresca is the more conservative theory everywhere, so its equivalent stress is never below the von Mises value, and von Mises therefore never reports the larger number. The two agree only in specific states — uniaxial tension being one — and differ by up to about 15% in pure shear, which is the largest gap. The relationship is geometric, set by the shapes of the two yield surfaces, so it does not depend on which ductile metal is involved.

quiz.q: A pure shear stress \( \tau = 50\ \mathrm{MPa} \) acts alone. What is the von Mises equivalent stress?
choices: \( 50\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 86.6\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 100\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 28.9\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
quiz.solution: With both normal stresses zero the formula reduces to \( \sigma' = \sqrt{3\tau^2} = \sqrt{3}\,\tau = 1.732\times50 = 86.6\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Answering 50 MPa treats shear as if it were directly comparable with a tensile strength, the error this lesson names explicitly. The 100 MPa answer doubles the shear, which is the Tresca result for this state and so belongs to the other theory. The 28.9 MPa answer divides by \( \sqrt{3} \) instead of multiplying, inverting the relation.

quiz.q: Under a static load on a ductile steel part, why is the stress-concentration factor \( K_t \) commonly set aside?
choices: Because \( K_t \) is always close to 1.0 for ductile metals
Because local yielding blunts and redistributes the peak stress
Because static loads are smaller than fatigue loads
Because \( K_t \) applies only to shear, not tension
quiz.solution: A ductile material yields locally at the notch, which redistributes load into the surrounding material and blunts the peak — the part tolerates the concentration rather than fracturing at it. \( K_t \) is a purely geometric factor and is routinely 2 to 3, nowhere near unity. The permission has nothing to do with load magnitude, and it is withdrawn entirely under fatigue or in brittle materials, where no redistribution mechanism exists. \( K_t \) applies to any stress type.

quiz.q: In a plane-stress state with principals \( 96.6 \) and \( -16.6\ \mathrm{MPa} \), what is the third principal stress used in the Tresca calculation?
choices: \( 96.6\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( -16.6\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 40\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
quiz.solution: Plane stress means the out-of-plane principal stress is zero, and it must still be included when identifying the maximum and minimum for Tresca. Here the set is \( \{96.6,\,0,\,-16.6\} \), so the Tresca stress is \( 96.6-(-16.6)=113.2\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Forgetting the zero is harmless when both in-plane principals straddle zero, as here, but becomes a real error when both are the same sign — in that case the zero is the minimum and governs the answer.

quiz.q: A designer reports "the factor of safety is 2.2" without naming a failure theory. What is the most accurate criticism?
choices: The number is meaningless because factors of safety are qualitative
The statement is incomplete: the same state gives different factors under different theories
The number is wrong because 2.2 is below the minimum permitted
No criticism — the theory does not affect the result
quiz.solution: The same stress state produced 2.36 by von Mises and 2.21 by Tresca in this lesson's worked example, so a bare factor of safety cannot be checked or compared against another engineer's number. The criticism is one of completeness, not of validity — the figure is perfectly meaningful once the theory is named. Nothing here establishes a minimum permitted value, and the claim that the theory does not matter is contradicted by the two results.

quiz.q: Which combination makes it mandatory to apply the stress-concentration factor in a static strength check?
choices: Ductile material, steady load
Brittle material, steady load
Ductile material, load applied slowly
Any material, provided the notch is small
quiz.solution: A brittle material cannot yield locally, so the geometric peak is the stress that actually acts and \( K_t \) must be carried through. Ductile materials under steady load redistribute the peak, which is the standard permission to set \( K_t \) aside; the rate of load application does not change that, since the mechanism is plasticity rather than strain rate. Notch size does not grant an exemption — a small sharp notch typically produces a higher \( K_t \), not a lower one.

quiz.q: Applying von Mises to a state with \( \sigma_x = 120\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( \sigma_y = 0 \), \( \tau_{xy} = 0 \) gives an equivalent stress of
choices: \( 120\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 208\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 60\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 69.3\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
quiz.solution: Uniaxial tension is the state the tension test itself produces, and any sound failure theory must return the applied stress unchanged there: \( \sqrt{120^2} = 120\ \mathrm{MPa} \). This is the sanity check to run on any failure-theory formula you are unsure you have remembered correctly — feed it uniaxial tension and see whether it hands the number back. The other options apply spurious factors of \( \sqrt{3} \) or one-half that have no term to attach to in this state.

quiz.q: The shear yield strength of a ductile steel with \( S_y = 300\ \mathrm{MPa} \), by the von Mises criterion, is approximately
choices: \( 300\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 173\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 150\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 520\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
quiz.solution: Von Mises gives \( S_{sy}=0.577\,S_y = 0.577\times300 = 173\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Using 300 MPa compares a shear stress against a tensile strength, the error worth roughly \( \sqrt{3} \) that this lesson flags. The 150 MPa answer is the Tresca prediction, \( S_y/2 \) — defensible if you say you used Tresca, but it is not the von Mises figure the question asks for. Multiplying by \( \sqrt{3} \) to reach 520 MPa moves in the wrong direction: shear capacity is always below tensile capacity.

2.kuwait: Applied case — a pin with a factor of three that was really 1.8. A lifting-lug pin on a maintenance davit is checked during a routine review. The original calculation divided the tensile yield strength by the pin's shear stress and reported a factor of safety of 3.1, which passed without comment for years. The reviewer repeats the check through von Mises: shear yield is \( 0.577 S_y \), and the real factor is 1.8. Nothing about the pin changed and no arithmetic was wrong — the original simply compared a shear stress against a tensile strength, two quantities that are not comparable. The lug was not replaced, because 1.8 was still adequate for its duty, but every other shear-loaded item in the same calculation package was rechecked, and two of them were not adequate. The lesson is that an error of kind propagates silently through a document in a way an error of arithmetic rarely does.
2.recap:
• Strength is quoted from a uniaxial tension test; real parts carry combined stress. A failure theory collapses a multiaxial state into one equivalent stress that can be compared against that single number honestly.
  • Von Mises: \( \sigma' = \sqrt{\sigma_x^2-\sigma_x\sigma_y+\sigma_y^2+3\tau_{xy}^2} \) — the most accurate predictor of yielding in ductile metals.
  • Tresca: \( \sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min} \) — always the more conservative, by up to about 15%, and never predicting a higher capacity than von Mises.
  • A factor of safety quoted without naming the theory used is an incomplete statement.
  • A discontinuity multiplies nominal stress geometrically: \( \sigma_{max}=K_t\sigma_{nom} \).
  • For a static load on a ductile material, local yielding blunts and redistributes the peak, so \( K_t \) is commonly set aside. That permission is withdrawn entirely for brittle materials and under fatigue — the bridge into Lesson 3.
  • Method: resolve the stress state at the worst point, get the principal stresses, name a theory, compare against \( S_y/n \), then decide whether \( K_t \) applies.
  • The commonest practical error is comparing a raw shear stress against a tensile yield strength — optimistic by roughly \( \sqrt3 \).

3.lecture:
§1 · Why static strength is not the answer

A shaft that never approaches yield can still fail, and usually does. Fatigue is damage accumulated by fluctuating stress: a crack initiates at a surface discontinuity, grows a little on each cycle, and severs the section at a nominal stress the static calculation declared safe by a wide margin. Most rotating-machinery failures are fatigue failures, and none of them are visible to a yield check.

§2 · The endurance limit and where it comes from

Test enough polished specimens and steels show a stress amplitude below which life becomes effectively unlimited — the endurance limit. For wrought steels a serviceable first estimate is \( S_e' = 0.5\,S_{ut} \) (capped near 700 MPa). The prime matters: that value belongs to a mirror-polished 7.6 mm rotating-bending specimen tested at room temperature, which is not the part you are designing.

§3 · The Marin factors — paying for reality

Key relation — corrected endurance limit

\[ S_e = k_a k_b k_c k_d k_e \, S_e' \]

\( k_a \) surface finish, \( k_b \) size, \( k_c \) load type, \( k_d \) temperature, \( k_e \) reliability. Each is at most 1.0, so they only ever reduce — and because they multiply, they stack fast.

Their physical logic is worth holding onto rather than memorising. Surface finish dominates because fatigue cracks start at the surface, so roughness supplies ready-made initiation sites: a machined finish costs about 17% at 600 MPa, and a hot-rolled or forged surface costs far more. Size reduces strength because a larger section exposes more highly-stressed volume, so the worst flaw present is statistically worse. Reliability is not a physical property at all but a choice about how far into the scatter band you design: 50% reliability means half of parts fail sooner than predicted, which is why 90%, 99% or 99.9% carry escalating penalties.

§4 · The estimating method

One: get \( S_{ut} \) for the actual material and condition, not the generic grade. Two: take \( S_e' = 0.5 S_{ut} \). Three: evaluate each Marin factor against the real part — its finish, its diameter, its loading, its service temperature, and the reliability the duty demands. Four: multiply. Five: compare the stress amplitude against \( S_e/n \), never the peak stress, because fatigue is driven by the alternating component. And carry \( K_f \), the fatigue concentration factor, always — the ductile-static permission of Lesson 2 does not survive here.

The characteristic number to remember is the size of the total knockdown. In the worked case below, five factors that each look modest combine to leave 58% of the specimen value. An engineer who designs to \( 0.5 S_{ut} \) directly is not being slightly optimistic; they are claiming nearly twice the fatigue strength the part has.

Closing. The endurance limit is a laboratory number until you have paid for your part's surface, size and required reliability. Then it is a design stress.

quiz.q:
What the specimen value costs after correction

Problem. A machined steel shaft of 30 mm diameter runs in rotating bending at room temperature. The steel has \( S_{ut} = 600\ \mathrm{MPa} \); the duty requires 99% reliability (\( k_e = 0.814 \)). Use \( k_a = 4.51\,S_{ut}^{-0.265} \) and \( k_b = 1.24\,d^{-0.107} \). Find: \( S_e' \), each Marin factor, and the corrected endurance limit \( S_e \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( S_e' = 0.5\times600 = 300\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) \( k_a = 4.51\times600^{-0.265} = 0.828 \). (3) \( k_b = 1.24\times30^{-0.107} = 0.862 \). (4) \( k_c = 1 \) (bending), \( k_d = 1 \) (room temperature), \( k_e = 0.814 \). (5) \( S_e = 0.828\times0.862\times1\times1\times0.814\times300 = 174.2\ \mathrm{MPa} \).

Answer: \( S_e \approx 174\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Sanity check: the total knockdown is \( 174.2/300 = 0.581 \) — the corrected limit is 58% of the specimen value, and 29% of \( S_{ut} \). Designing against \( 0.5S_{ut} = 300 \) would have claimed 1.72 times the fatigue strength this shaft actually possesses.

quiz.q:
Buying strength with surface finish

Problem. The same shaft is ground rather than machined, so \( k_a = 1.58\,S_{ut}^{-0.085} \). All other factors are unchanged. Find: the new \( k_a \), the new \( S_e \), and the percentage gain in endurance limit.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( k_a = 1.58\times600^{-0.085} = 0.917 \). (2) \( S_e = 0.917\times0.862\times0.814\times300 = 193.0\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (3) Gain: \( 193.0/174.2 - 1 = 0.108 \), i.e. 10.8%.

Answer: \( k_a = 0.917 \), \( S_e = 193\ \mathrm{MPa} \), a 10.8% gain. Sanity check: grinding buys about a tenth more fatigue strength for one extra manufacturing operation — often the cheapest strength available, and far cheaper than the larger diameter that would otherwise be needed. It is also why a drawing note specifying surface finish in a fillet is a structural requirement, not cosmetic.

quiz.q:
Amplitude, not peak

Problem. A component cycles between \( \sigma_{min} = 20\ \mathrm{MPa} \) and \( \sigma_{max} = 140\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Find: the stress amplitude and mean stress, and the factor of safety on infinite life against \( S_e = 174\ \mathrm{MPa} \), ignoring the mean-stress effect for now.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Amplitude: \( \sigma_a = (140-20)/2 = 60\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) Mean: \( \sigma_m = (140+20)/2 = 80\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (3) \( n = S_e/\sigma_a = 174/60 = 2.9 \).

Answer: \( \sigma_a = 60 \), \( \sigma_m = 80\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( n = 2.9 \). Sanity check: comparing the peak 140 MPa against \( S_e \) instead would have reported \( n = 1.24 \) — needlessly alarming — while ignoring that the 80 MPa mean stress is itself damaging in a way this calculation has not yet accounted for. Lesson 4 supplies the Goodman treatment that reconciles the two.

quiz.q: For a wrought steel with \( S_{ut} = 800\ \mathrm{MPa} \), the first estimate of the specimen endurance limit \( S_e' \) is
choices: \( 400\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 800\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 240\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 1600\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
quiz.solution: The standard first estimate for wrought steel is \( S_e' = 0.5\,S_{ut} = 400\ \mathrm{MPa} \), subject to the cap near 700 MPa that applies to very high-strength steels. Answering 800 MPa confuses the endurance limit with the ultimate strength itself. The 240 MPa figure applies 0.3 rather than 0.5, and 1600 MPa doubles instead of halving — fatigue strength is always below static strength, so any answer above \( S_{ut} \) can be rejected on sight.

quiz.q: Which Marin factor is typically the largest single knockdown for an as-forged component?
choices: Size, \( k_b \)
Surface finish, \( k_a \)
Load type, \( k_c \)
Temperature, \( k_d \)
quiz.solution: Fatigue cracks initiate at the surface, so surface condition dominates: a rough as-forged skin supplies ready-made initiation sites and can cut the endurance limit by more than half on a strong steel. Size is real but milder over ordinary shaft diameters — around 0.86 at 30 mm. Load type applies a fixed adjustment for axial or torsional loading rather than a finish-dependent one, and temperature is 1.0 until the part runs hot. This ranking is why grinding a fillet is such a cost-effective structural intervention.

quiz.q: Five Marin factors of 0.83, 0.86, 1.0, 1.0 and 0.81 are applied to \( S_e' = 300\ \mathrm{MPa} \). The corrected endurance limit is closest to
choices: \( 300\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 174\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 250\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
\( 90\ \mathrm{MPa} \)
quiz.solution: The factors multiply: \( 0.83\times0.86\times0.81 = 0.578 \), and \( 0.578\times300 \approx 174\ \mathrm{MPa} \). The 250 MPa answer comes from averaging the factors instead of multiplying, which badly understates the stacking; 300 MPa ignores the correction entirely. The 90 MPa answer roughly adds the shortfalls rather than compounding the factors, over-penalising the part. Multiplication is the point: several individually modest factors combine to remove more than 40% of the specimen value.

quiz.q: Fatigue design compares which stress quantity against the corrected endurance limit?
choices: The maximum stress in the cycle
The stress amplitude
The mean stress
The static yield stress
quiz.solution: Fatigue damage is driven by the alternating component, so the stress amplitude \( \sigma_a = (\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min})/2 \) is the quantity compared against \( S_e \). Using the maximum stress conflates the steady and fluctuating parts and reports a needlessly low factor of safety. The mean stress is not ignored — it genuinely reduces allowable amplitude — but it enters through a Goodman or Gerber construction rather than by direct comparison. The yield stress governs a different failure mode entirely.

quiz.q: Raising the required reliability from 50% to 99% changes \( k_e \) from 1.000 to 0.814. What does this represent physically?
choices: The material becomes weaker at higher reliability
A choice about how far into the strength scatter band the design sits
An allowance for higher operating temperature
A correction for the larger size of reliable parts
quiz.solution: Reliability is not a property of the material but a decision about scatter. The endurance limit measured across many specimens is a distribution; designing at 50% reliability means half of parts are expected to fail earlier than predicted, which is rarely acceptable, so the design stress is moved down the distribution and \( k_e \) falls. The steel is unchanged. Temperature is handled separately by \( k_d \), and size by \( k_b \); neither has anything to do with the reliability choice.

quiz.q: Why must the fatigue stress-concentration factor be carried through a fatigue calculation, when \( K_t \) is often set aside for static ductile design?
choices: Fatigue loads are always larger than static loads
Local yielding cannot blunt a peak that recurs every cycle at the crack initiation site
\( K_t \) is only defined for cyclic loading
Fatigue calculations use nominal stress, so the factor compensates
quiz.solution: The static permission rests on local yielding redistributing the peak once. Under cyclic loading the notch root is exactly where a crack initiates and then grows a little on every cycle, so the concentration governs the life rather than being blunted away. Fatigue loads are typically smaller than the static ones a part survives, which is what makes fatigue failures surprising. \( K_t \) is a purely geometric factor defined regardless of loading, and the last option inverts the logic of nominal stress.

quiz.q: A shaft's diameter is increased from 30 mm to 60 mm. Using \( k_b = 1.24\,d^{-0.107} \), the size factor
choices: increases, because a bigger shaft is stronger
decreases slightly, because more highly-stressed material is exposed
is unchanged, because \( k_b \) depends only on material
halves, in proportion to the diameter
quiz.solution: The exponent is negative, so \( k_b \) falls as diameter grows: from 0.862 at 30 mm to about 0.800 at 60 mm, a reduction of roughly 7%. The physical reason is statistical — a larger section exposes a greater volume of highly-stressed material, so the worst flaw present is likely to be worse. Note this concerns strength per unit area: the bigger shaft still carries far more load, because section modulus grows with the cube of diameter while \( k_b \) declines only weakly. The factor certainly depends on geometry, and the decline is nothing like proportional.

quiz.q: A designer sizes a machined 30 mm shaft directly against \( 0.5\,S_{ut} \), omitting the Marin factors. Compared with the corrected value of 174 MPa, the claimed fatigue strength is too high by a factor of about
choices: 1.0 — the omission is harmless
quiz.solution: The claim is 300 MPa against an actual 174 MPa, a ratio of \( 300/174 = 1.72 \). This is the practical significance of the whole lesson: the omission is not a rounding matter but nearly a factor of two, and it is invisible in the arithmetic because every individual step is correct. A part designed this way can pass every check in the calculation package and still fail in service, which is precisely the pattern that makes fatigue the dominant failure mode in rotating machinery.

3.kuwait: Applied case — the shaft that passed every static check. A cooling-water pump shaft fails through a keyway after eighteen months. The original calculation is retrieved and is arithmetically flawless: peak stress well below yield, factor of safety above four. It contains no fatigue check at all. Re-worked under this lesson's method, the picture inverts — the corrected endurance limit for the machined 30 mm section at 99% reliability is about 174 MPa, not the 300 MPa a bare \( 0.5S_{ut} \) would have claimed, and the keyway's fatigue concentration applies in full because the ductile-static permission does not survive cyclic loading. The replacement shaft is ground at the fillet and the keyway radius increased; both changes buy fatigue strength rather than section. The instructive part is that no one made a calculation error. They answered the wrong question, thoroughly.
3.recap:
• A part that never approaches yield can still fail: fatigue accumulates damage under fluctuating stress, and most rotating-machinery failures are fatigue failures invisible to a yield check.
  • For wrought steels a first estimate of the specimen endurance limit is \( S_e' = 0.5S_{ut} \), capped near 700 MPa — a mirror-polished laboratory value, not a design stress.
  • The Marin factors correct it to the real part: \( S_e = k_ak_bk_ck_dk_e S_e' \). Each is at most 1.0, and because they multiply they stack fast.
  • Surface finish dominates, because fatigue cracks start at the surface and roughness supplies ready-made initiation sites. Size punishes the larger stressed volume; reliability is a choice about where in the scatter band you design, not a material property.
  • On the worked 30 mm machined shaft, five modest factors left 58% of the specimen value — \( S_e = 174 \) MPa against \( S_e' = 300 \).
  • Compare the stress amplitude against \( S_e/n \), never the peak: fatigue is driven by the alternating component.
  • Carry \( K_f \) always — the ductile-static permission of Lesson 2 does not survive cyclic loading, because the notch root is where the crack grows a little on every cycle.
  • Designing directly against \( 0.5S_{ut} \) claims about 1.7 times the fatigue strength the part actually has, with every individual arithmetic step correct.

4.lecture:
§1 · The gap Lesson 3 left open

Lesson 3 finished with a factor of safety of 2.9 on a component cycling between 20 and 140 MPa, and flagged the omission plainly: the calculation compared the amplitude against \( S_e \) and ignored the 80 MPa mean stress entirely. That mean stress is not harmless. A steady tensile load holds a crack open, so each cycle does more damage than the same amplitude would about zero mean. Fatigue strength therefore depends on two numbers, and a one-dimensional comparison cannot express the answer.

§2 · Constant-life criteria

The standard treatment plots mean stress horizontally and amplitude vertically, and draws a boundary between the survivable region and the rest. Every criterion in use passes through the same two anchors — \( S_e \) on the amplitude axis, where there is no mean stress, and \( S_{ut} \) on the mean axis, where there is no alternation and the part simply pulls apart. They differ only in the curve drawn between them.

Key relation — the Goodman criterion

\[ \frac{\sigma_a}{S_e} + \frac{\sigma_m}{S_{ut}} = \frac{1}{n} \]

A straight line between the two anchors. Gerber replaces the second term with \( (\sigma_m/S_{ut})^2 \), bulging above the line; Soderberg replaces \( S_{ut} \) with the yield strength \( S_y \), pulling below it. Setting \( \sigma_m = 0 \) collapses all three to \( n = S_e/\sigma_a \) — Lesson 3's calculation, recovered exactly.

Which to use is a judgement, not a lookup. Goodman is linear, always conservative against test data, and trivially invertible for design — which is why it dominates practice. Gerber follows the experimental scatter band more closely and returns a less punishing answer: on the worked case below, 2.56 against Goodman's 2.09, a 22% difference that is real money in material. Soderberg alone guarantees no yielding at the first peak, because it is anchored at \( S_y \), but it is conservative enough that most designers run Goodman for fatigue and a separate first-cycle yield check instead.

§3 · Variable amplitude and Miner's rule

Real duty is not one amplitude. A crane hoists light loads often and heavy loads rarely; a pump shaft sees startup transients on top of running load. The standard accounting device is the Palmgren–Miner rule: each block of \( n_i \) cycles at an amplitude whose life is \( N_i \) consumes the fraction \( n_i/N_i \), and failure is predicted when the fractions sum to one.

Key relation — cumulative damage

\[ D = \sum_i \frac{n_i}{N_i} \qquad \text{failure predicted at } D = 1 \]

\( N_i \) comes from the finite-life line \( S_f = a N^{\,b} \), fitted between \( 0.9 S_{ut} \) at \( 10^3 \) cycles and \( S_e \) at \( 10^6 \).

§4 · Miner's rule is known to be wrong

It is worth being blunt about this, because the rule is used everywhere and defended nowhere. Miner's rule assumes damage accumulates linearly and independently of order. Neither is true. Test data puts failure anywhere from \( D \approx 0.5 \) to \( D \approx 2 \), and sequence matters: a few high-amplitude cycles early can drive a crack that subsequent low-amplitude cycles then extend, whereas the same high cycles applied last may find nothing to grow. A large overload can even be beneficial, leaving a compressive residual stress at the notch root that retards later growth.

The rule survives because it is simple, because it is roughly unbiased across many tests, and because nothing appreciably better is available without crack-growth analysis. Use it — and treat a computed \( D \) of 0.9 as "no margin demonstrated", not as "passed".

Closing. Mean stress costs amplitude, and the constant-life diagram is where that trade is priced. Variable duty is summed with Miner's rule, whose answer is an estimate with a factor of two around it, not a number to design to the last digit.

Glossary

Gerber criterion\( n\sigma_a/S_e + (n\sigma_m/S_{ut})^2 = 1 \)When a less punishing, better-centred estimate is wanted and the extra algebra is acceptable.

quiz.q:
What the mean stress actually costs

Problem. Lesson 3 left a component cycling between \( \sigma_{min}=20 \) and \( \sigma_{max}=140\ \mathrm{MPa} \) with a reported factor of safety of 2.9 against \( S_e = 174\ \mathrm{MPa} \), the mean stress ignored. The steel has \( S_{ut}=600\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Find: the factor of safety by Goodman and by Gerber, and say what the mean stress cost.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( \sigma_a=(140-20)/2=60 \), \( \sigma_m=(140+20)/2=80\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) Goodman: \( 60/174 + 80/600 = 0.3448+0.1333=0.4782 \), so \( n=1/0.4782=2.09 \). (3) Gerber: solve \( 0.3448\,n + (0.1333\,n)^2 = 1 \), i.e. \( 0.01778n^2+0.3448n-1=0 \), giving \( n=2.56 \).

Answer: Goodman \( n=2.09 \), Gerber \( n=2.56 \). Sanity check: both are below Lesson 3's 2.9, as they must be — adding a damaging mean stress cannot raise the margin. Goodman costs 28% of the mean-free answer and Gerber 12%. Setting \( \sigma_m=0 \) in either expression returns exactly 2.90, which is the arithmetic confirming the two lessons agree where they overlap.

quiz.q:
Adding up a duty cycle

Problem. A shaft of the same steel (\( S_{ut}=600 \), \( S_e=174\ \mathrm{MPa} \)) sees, per year: 10,000 cycles at 300 MPa amplitude, 30,000 at 250 MPa, and 100,000 at 200 MPa, all fully reversed. Fit the finite-life line between \( 0.9S_{ut} \) at \( 10^3 \) cycles and \( S_e \) at \( 10^6 \). Find: the annual damage \( D \), and how many years of this duty Miner's rule allows.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Endpoints: \( 0.9\times600=540\ \mathrm{MPa} \) at \( 10^3 \), \( 174\ \mathrm{MPa} \) at \( 10^6 \). (2) \( b=-\tfrac13\log_{10}(540/174)=-0.1639 \); \( a=540^2/174=1675.9\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (3) Lives from \( N=(S_f/a)^{1/b} \): at 300 MPa, \( N=36{,}060 \); at 250 MPa, \( N=109{,}647 \); at 200 MPa, \( N=427{,}660 \). (4) \( D = 10{,}000/36{,}060 + 30{,}000/109{,}647 + 100{,}000/427{,}660 = 0.2773+0.2736+0.2338 = 0.785 \). (5) Years to \( D=1 \): \( 1/0.785 = 1.27 \).

Answer: \( D=0.785 \) per year; failure predicted at about 1.3 years. Sanity check: the line is verified at its own endpoint — \( 1675.9\times(10^6)^{-0.1639}=174.0\ \mathrm{MPa} \), the corrected endurance limit it was fitted to. Note how evenly the three blocks contribute, 0.23 to 0.28 each: the rare high-amplitude cycles do as much damage as the hundred thousand mild ones, which is exactly the intuition a running-load-only calculation lacks.

quiz.q:
Designing to a target margin

Problem. The same steel and \( S_e=174\ \mathrm{MPa} \). A joint carries an unavoidable mean stress of 80 MPa and must show a Goodman factor of safety of 2.0. Find: the largest stress amplitude permitted, and the peak stress that corresponds to.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Rearranging Goodman for amplitude: \( \sigma_a = S_e\left(\tfrac1n - \tfrac{\sigma_m}{S_{ut}}\right) \). (2) \( \sigma_a = 174\,(0.5 - 80/600) = 174\times0.3667 = 63.8\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (3) Peak: \( \sigma_{max} = \sigma_m+\sigma_a = 80+63.8 = 143.8\ \mathrm{MPa} \).

Answer: \( \sigma_a \le 63.8\ \mathrm{MPa} \), peak 143.8 MPa. Sanity check: substituting back, \( 63.8/174 + 80/600 = 0.3667+0.1333 = 0.500 = 1/2 \) — the target margin exactly. Note the peak stress of 144 MPa is a quarter of \( S_{ut} \) and well under any plausible yield strength: the part is nowhere near static failure, which is the ordinary condition of a fatigue-governed design.

quiz.q: On a constant-life diagram, the Goodman line runs between which two anchor points?
choices: \( S_y \) on the amplitude axis and \( S_{ut} \) on the mean axis
\( S_e \) on the amplitude axis and \( S_{ut} \) on the mean axis
\( S_e \) on both axes
\( 0.5S_{ut} \) on the amplitude axis and \( S_y \) on the mean axis
quiz.solution: With no mean stress the part survives an amplitude of \( S_e \), fixing the vertical anchor; with no alternation it is a static tensile member that fails at \( S_{ut} \), fixing the horizontal one. Soderberg is the criterion that anchors at \( S_y \) instead, and it does so on the mean axis, not the amplitude axis. Using \( 0.5S_{ut} \) would put the uncorrected specimen value on the diagram, discarding the Marin factors Lesson 3 spent its length establishing.

quiz.q: A component has \( \sigma_a = 90 \) and \( \sigma_m = 150\ \mathrm{MPa} \), with \( S_e = 174 \) and \( S_{ut} = 600\ \mathrm{MPa} \). The Goodman factor of safety is closest to
quiz.solution: \( 90/174 + 150/600 = 0.5172 + 0.2500 = 0.7672 \), and \( n = 1/0.7672 = 1.30 \). The 1.93 answer is \( S_e/\sigma_a \), the mean stress ignored — the very error this lesson exists to correct. The 0.77 figure is the sum itself, which is \( 1/n \) and not the margin. A margin of 1.30 on a fatigue calculation is thin: the inputs carry more scatter than that.

quiz.q: Compared with Goodman, the Gerber criterion generally
choices: predicts a lower factor of safety for the same load
predicts a higher factor of safety, following the test scatter more closely
gives an identical answer whenever \( \sigma_m > 0 \)
applies only to brittle materials
quiz.solution: Gerber's parabola bulges above Goodman's straight line everywhere between the two shared anchors, so it permits more amplitude at a given mean stress and returns the larger margin — 2.56 against 2.09 on this lesson's worked case. That is the point of it: the straight line is a deliberately conservative simplification of a data set the parabola sits centrally within. The two agree only at the anchors themselves, where \( \sigma_m \) is zero or \( \sigma_a \) is zero.

quiz.q: Which criterion is the one that guarantees no yielding on the first load cycle?
choices: Goodman
Gerber
Soderberg
Miner
quiz.solution: Soderberg anchors the mean-stress axis at \( S_y \) rather than \( S_{ut} \), so satisfying it necessarily keeps \( \sigma_m + \sigma_a \) below yield. Goodman and Gerber both anchor at \( S_{ut} \) and can therefore pass a combination that yields locally on the first cycle, which is why they are normally run alongside a separate static yield check. Miner is not a constant-life criterion at all — it is the damage-summation rule for variable amplitude.

quiz.q: A duty spectrum gives \( n_1/N_1 = 0.45 \) and \( n_2/N_2 = 0.40 \). Miner's rule predicts
choices: failure, because two blocks were applied
survival with \( D = 0.85 \), though with little demonstrated margin
survival with \( D = 0.18 \)
nothing, because the blocks have different amplitudes
quiz.solution: The fractions add: \( D = 0.45+0.40 = 0.85 \), below the predicted failure value of 1. The 0.18 answer multiplies them, which has no physical meaning. Miner's rule exists precisely to combine blocks of different amplitude, so the last option inverts its purpose. The honest reading of 0.85 is that the design has consumed most of its predicted life with the rule's own scatter — roughly 0.5 to 2 — wider than the remaining 0.15.

quiz.q: Why can the order in which load blocks are applied change the actual life, contrary to Miner's assumption?
choices: Because the material's \( S_{ut} \) changes with load history
Because early high-amplitude cycles can start a crack that later mild cycles extend, and a large overload can leave a retarding compressive residual stress
Because \( N_i \) is measured only for constant-amplitude tests
Because damage fractions are dimensionless
quiz.solution: Sequence matters through the crack itself. High cycles applied early initiate damage that subsequent low-amplitude cycles — which alone might never start a crack — are perfectly able to grow; applied last, the same cycles may find nothing to extend. Separately, a single large overload can yield the notch root and leave a compressive residual stress there that retards later growth, so an overload can lengthen life. Neither effect exists in a linear sum. The ultimate strength is not altered by this, and the dimensionlessness of \( D \) is beside the point.

quiz.q: A finite-life line is fitted between 540 MPa at \( 10^3 \) cycles and 174 MPa at \( 10^6 \) cycles. The exponent \( b \) is closest to
quiz.solution: \( b = -\tfrac13\log_{10}(540/174) = -\tfrac13(0.4916) = -0.164 \). The \( -0.492 \) answer omits the factor of one third, which is the three decades of life between the endpoints. A positive exponent would make fatigue strength rise with life, which is backwards. The \( -3.00 \) figure inverts the relationship — it is roughly \( 1/b \), the exponent used when solving for \( N \) from a known stress rather than the reverse.

quiz.q: A designer reports a Goodman margin of 2.09 and a Gerber margin of 2.56 for the same component and asks which to put in the calculation package. The defensible answer is
choices: Gerber, because it is the more accurate criterion
Goodman, stating the criterion used — the choice is a documented judgement, and the conservative line is the normal default
The average of the two
Whichever exceeds the required margin
quiz.solution: What makes a fatigue number defensible is that the criterion is named and the inputs are traceable, not that a particular curve was chosen. Goodman is the ordinary default because it is conservative against the data and invertible for design, so it is the natural entry — with Gerber available as the argued case if the extra 22% is needed and justified. Averaging two criteria produces a curve nobody has validated. Choosing whichever clears the target is selecting the answer first and the method afterwards, which is the one approach that cannot be defended in review.

4.kuwait: Applied case — the duty cycle nobody added up. A reciprocating-compressor tie rod is specified against its running load and passes comfortably. It fails after three years. The running load was never the problem: the rod also sees a startup transient at roughly 300 MPa amplitude, a few thousand cycles per year of unloaded-to-loaded transition near 250 MPa, and the steady running cycles near 200 MPa. Each block on its own is survivable — the 200 MPa duty alone would run past four hundred thousand cycles. Summed with Miner's rule the annual damage comes to 0.78, which is not a pass; it means the rod is predicted to fail somewhere in the second year of identical duty, and the observed three years sits inside the rule's normal factor-of-two scatter. Two changes follow. The startup ramp is lengthened so the transient amplitude drops, which is free, and the rod is re-specified with a rolled rather than cut thread, which raises \( S_e \) and lengthens every block at once. The instructive part is that the original calculation was not wrong about any single load. It simply never asked what the loads did together.
4.recap:
• A tensile mean stress reduces the amplitude a part can survive, so a fatigue state needs two coordinates — \( \sigma_a \) and \( \sigma_m \) — not one.
  • Constant-life criteria all run between \( S_e \) on the amplitude axis and \( S_{ut} \) on the mean axis. Goodman is the straight line between them: \( \sigma_a/S_e + \sigma_m/S_{ut} = 1/n \).
  • Gerber's parabola is less conservative (2.56 vs Goodman's 2.09 on this lesson's case); Soderberg anchors at \( S_y \) and alone rules out first-cycle yielding.
  • Setting \( \sigma_m = 0 \) returns every criterion to \( n = S_e/\sigma_a \), Lesson 3's result.
  • Variable-amplitude duty is summed with Miner's rule, \( D=\sum n_i/N_i \), with lives read off the finite-life line \( S_f = aN^{\,b} \).
  • Miner's rule ignores load order and real failures scatter between \( D\approx0.5 \) and \( D\approx2 \). Treat \( D=0.9 \) as no demonstrated margin.

5.lecture:
§1 · Why shafts get their own method

A shaft is where this course's first four lessons arrive together. It carries bending and torsion at once, so Lesson 2's combined-stress work applies; it turns, so Lesson 3's fatigue correction applies; and its torque is usually steady while its bending is not, so Lesson 4's mean-stress treatment applies to the two loads differently. That last point is the one worth slowing down for.

Consider a fibre on the surface of a rotating shaft under a fixed transverse load. Half a revolution later that same fibre is on the other side of the neutral axis. The bending stress it sees is therefore fully reversed: \( \sigma_m = 0 \) and \( \sigma_a = 32M/\pi d^3 \). The torque, meanwhile, does not care where the fibre is — a steadily driven pump applies the same torque continuously, so the shear stress is steady: \( \tau_a = 0 \) and \( \tau_m = 16T/\pi d^3 \). One shaft, one speed, two completely different fatigue characters.

§2 · Assembling the design equation

Combine each pair into a von Mises equivalent — amplitude from the bending, mean from the torsion — and substitute into Goodman. Since \( \sigma'_a = \sigma_a \) for pure reversed bending and \( \sigma'_m = \sqrt3\,\tau_m \) for pure steady torsion, Goodman becomes an equation in \( d^3 \) that inverts cleanly.

Key relation — DE-Goodman shaft diameter

\[ d^3 = \frac{16n}{\pi}\left[\frac{2K_f M_a}{S_e} + \frac{\sqrt3\,K_{fs} T_m}{S_{ut}}\right] \]

\( M_a \) the alternating bending moment, \( T_m \) the steady torque, \( K_f \) and \( K_{fs} \) the fatigue concentration factors in bending and torsion at the section being sized. Every term is a moment over a strength, so the bracket has units of volume and the cube root returns a length.

Two habits make this equation safe. First, size at the critical section, not the section of maximum moment — a shoulder or keyway a little away from the peak often governs, because \( K_f \) there can outweigh the smaller moment. Second, note that \( d \) responds to the cube root of everything: doubling the factor of safety enlarges the shaft by only 26%. Fatigue margin on a shaft is cheap in diameter and expensive in nothing else, which is why shafts are rarely the component worth trimming.

§3 · The checks strength does not cover

A shaft sized for stress can still be unfit. Deflection is the usual first offender: gears mesh badly and bearings run at an angle if the shaft bends too far, so slope at each bearing is normally held to around 0.001 rad and gear-mesh deflection to a small fraction of a module. These are stiffness limits, and stiffness depends on \( d^4 \) and on \( E \) — which means a stronger steel does not help at all, since every steel has essentially the same modulus.

The second is critical speed. A shaft with mass on it is a spring-mass system that will resonate at \( \omega_n = \sqrt{k/m} \). Run at that speed and deflection grows until something limits it, usually the shaft. The first critical speed must sit well clear of the operating range — a common rule keeps the operating speed below about three-quarters of the first critical.

Key relation — first critical speed

\[ \omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{g}{\delta}}, \qquad k=\frac{48EI}{L^3} \ \text{(central mass, simple supports)} \]

The two forms are the same statement: \( \delta = mg/k \) is the static deflection under the mass, so a shaft that barely sags has a high critical speed. A useful field check needs nothing but a dial indicator.

§4 · Detailing, where the fatigue life is actually decided

The diameter is the easy part. What survives or does not is the detail. A shoulder is a stress raiser whose \( K_f \) depends almost entirely on the fillet radius, so the drawing note specifying that radius is a structural requirement — a sharp corner where a generous radius was intended can move \( K_f \) from 1.5 to well past 2. A keyway is worse, typically 2.0 or more in bending, and it sits exactly where torque is transferred. Press fits raise the concentration at the end of the hub. Surface finish enters through \( k_a \), which is why grinding a fillet is such a good return, as Lesson 3's worked case showed.

The practical consequence: when a shaft calculation comes out marginal, the cheapest fixes are usually not more diameter. Increase the fillet radius, grind the critical section, move the keyway away from the peak moment, or use a splined or interference-fit torque path instead. Each buys fatigue strength without buying steel.

Closing. Reversed bending and steady torque enter the fatigue criterion through different terms; that asymmetry is the shaft equation. Then check deflection and critical speed, which strength never covers, and detail the fillets and keyways as if the life depends on them, because it does.

What this lesson assumes

  • Bending and torsional stress formulae (Strength of Materials L2–L4) — \( \sigma=32M/\pi d^3 \) and \( \tau=16T/\pi d^3 \) for solid round sections.
  • Von Mises equivalent stress (Lesson 2) — how a bending–torsion state collapses to one number for comparison against a strength.
  • Corrected endurance limit (Lesson 3) — \( S_e \), the amplitude-side denominator.
  • Goodman criterion (Lesson 4) — the mean-stress treatment the shaft equation is derived from.
  • Natural frequency of a spring–mass system (Physics I / Dynamics) — \( \omega_n=\sqrt{k/m} \), reused here as critical speed.
