quiz.q:
Sizing the pump shaft

Problem. A pump shaft transmits 15 kW at 1450 rpm and carries a peak bending moment of 250 N·m at the impeller hub. The steel is the course's usual \( S_{ut}=600\ \mathrm{MPa} \) with a corrected \( S_e=174\ \mathrm{MPa} \). At the critical shoulder \( K_f=1.8 \) and \( K_{fs}=1.5 \). Design for \( n=2.0 \). Find: the transmitted torque and the required diameter.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( \omega = 1450\times2\pi/60 = 151.84\ \mathrm{rad/s} \), so \( T = P/\omega = 15{,}000/151.84 = 98.8\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (2) Amplitude term: \( 2K_fM_a/S_e = 2(1.8)(250)/174\times10^6 = 5.172\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3} \). (3) Mean term: \( \sqrt3 K_{fs}T_m/S_{ut} = 1.732(1.5)(98.8)/600\times10^6 = 4.278\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^3} \). (4) \( d^3 = (16\times2/\pi)(5.172\times10^{-6}+4.278\times10^{-7}) = 10.186\times5.600\times10^{-6} = 5.704\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3} \). (5) \( d = 38.5\ \mathrm{mm} \) — specify the next standard size, 40 mm.

Answer: \( T=98.8\ \mathrm{N\,m} \), \( d=38.5\ \mathrm{mm} \), specified as 40 mm. Sanity check: the bending term is twelve times the torsion term, so this shaft is bending-governed and the torque is almost incidental to the size — worth knowing before anyone proposes trimming the shaft to save on a torque re-rate. Back-substituting the specified 40 mm gives \( \sigma_a=71.6 \) and \( \sqrt3\tau_m=20.4\ \mathrm{MPa} \), a Goodman margin of 2.24 — the rounding up to a standard size bought 12% of extra margin for nothing.

quiz.q:
What a keyway costs

Problem. The same shaft, but a keyway at the critical section raises the bending fatigue concentration from \( K_f=1.8 \) to \( K_f=2.2 \). Everything else is unchanged. Find: the new required diameter, and express the penalty as a percentage of diameter and of cross-sectional area.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) New amplitude term: \( 2(2.2)(250)/174\times10^6 = 6.322\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3} \). (2) \( d^3 = 10.186\,(6.322\times10^{-6}+4.278\times10^{-7}) = 6.876\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3} \), so \( d = 41.0\ \mathrm{mm} \). (3) Diameter penalty: \( 41.0/38.5-1 = 6.4\% \). Area penalty: \( 1.064^2-1 = 13.3\% \).

Answer: \( d=41.0\ \mathrm{mm} \) — a 6.4% diameter and 13.3% area penalty. Sanity check: a 22% rise in \( K_f \) produced only a 6.4% rise in diameter, which is the cube root at work again. Read it the other way, though, and it is a warning: the same cube root means a detailing error that quietly doubles \( K_f \) is not absorbed by a shaft sized with a margin of two. It is exactly the kind of change that consumes a margin nobody notices being spent.

quiz.q:
Is it clear of resonance?

Problem. The 40 mm shaft spans 500 mm between bearings and carries a 20 kg impeller at midspan. Take \( E=207\ \mathrm{GPa} \) and treat the supports as simple, so \( k=48EI/L^3 \). Find: the shaft stiffness, the first critical speed in rpm, and the margin over the 1450 rpm operating speed.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( I=\pi d^4/64 = \pi(0.040)^4/64 = 1.2566\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^4} \). (2) \( k = 48(207\times10^9)(1.2566\times10^{-7})/(0.500)^3 = 9.989\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N/m} \). (3) \( \omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}=\sqrt{9.989\times10^6/20}=706.7\ \mathrm{rad/s} \). (4) \( N_c = 706.7\times60/2\pi = 6749\ \mathrm{rpm} \). (5) Margin: \( 6749/1450 = 4.65 \).

Answer: \( k=9.99\ \mathrm{MN/m} \), \( N_c=6749\ \mathrm{rpm} \), 4.65 times the operating speed. Sanity check: the static deflection under the impeller is \( \delta=mg/k=20(9.81)/9.989\times10^6=0.0196\ \mathrm{mm} \), and the independent form \( \omega_n=\sqrt{g/\delta}=\sqrt{9.81/1.96\times10^{-5}}=706.7\ \mathrm{rad/s} \) — the same answer from a completely different route, which is the check worth doing. A shaft that sags twenty microns is nowhere near resonance.

quiz.q: On a rotating shaft carrying a fixed transverse load and a steadily driven torque, the bending and torsional stresses are respectively
choices: both fully reversed
bending fully reversed, torsion steady
bending steady, torsion fully reversed
both steady
quiz.solution: A surface fibre travels from the tension side to the compression side once per revolution, so bending is fully reversed — that is what rotation does to a fixed load. The torque, by contrast, is applied continuously by the driver and does not depend on angular position, so the shear stress is steady. This asymmetry is the entire reason the shaft equation puts \( M_a \) over \( S_e \) and \( T_m \) over \( S_{ut} \) rather than treating both loads alike.

quiz.q: In the DE-Goodman shaft equation, the torque term is divided by \( S_{ut} \) rather than \( S_e \) because
choices: torsion is always less damaging than bending
the torque is a steady mean stress, and Goodman puts mean stress over \( S_{ut} \)
\( S_e \) is not defined for shear
the factor \( \sqrt3 \) already accounts for it
quiz.solution: The denominators are not a ranking of which load is nastier — they follow directly from the Goodman criterion of Lesson 4, where the amplitude term carries \( S_e \) and the mean term carries \( S_{ut} \). A steady torque contributes only mean stress, so it lands in the second term. If the torque did fluctuate, its alternating part would move into the \( S_e \) term alongside the bending. The \( \sqrt3 \) is a separate matter: it converts a shear stress to its von Mises equivalent.

quiz.q: A shaft sized for a factor of safety of 2 is re-specified for a factor of safety of 4, all loads unchanged. The diameter increases by about
quiz.solution: \( d \propto n^{1/3} \), so doubling \( n \) multiplies the diameter by \( 2^{1/3}=1.26 \) — a 26% increase. The 100% answer treats the relation as linear and 41% uses a square root. This cube-root behaviour is why fatigue margin on a shaft is unusually cheap to buy: doubling the margin costs a quarter more diameter and about 59% more steel by weight, which on a pump shaft is a trivial sum against the cost of a failure.

quiz.q: A shaft passes its fatigue check comfortably but gears mounted on it mesh badly and bearings run hot. The most likely omission is
choices: a stronger steel was needed
a deflection and slope check
the endurance limit was not corrected
the torque was underestimated
quiz.solution: These are stiffness symptoms, not strength ones. Bearing slope is normally held near 0.001 rad and gear-mesh deflection to a fraction of a module, and neither limit appears anywhere in a stress calculation. The reason a stronger steel does not help is worth holding onto: deflection depends on \( E \) and \( I \), and every steel has essentially the same modulus, so the only fixes are more diameter or a shorter span.

quiz.q: Two shafts are identical except that one is made from a steel with twice the yield strength. Their first critical speeds are
choices: in the ratio 2:1
in the ratio \( \sqrt2 \):1
essentially equal
in the ratio 1:2
quiz.solution: Critical speed follows \( \omega_n=\sqrt{k/m} \) with \( k=48EI/L^3 \) — elastic modulus, second moment of area, span and mass. Strength does not appear. Since all steels share a modulus near 200 GPa, the stronger steel gives essentially the same critical speed. The same reasoning explains why a resonance problem is never solved by a material upgrade: change the geometry, the span, or the mass.

quiz.q: A 40 mm shaft on 500 mm simple supports deflects 0.0196 mm under its central mass. Its first critical speed is closest to
choices: \( 700\ \mathrm{rpm} \)
\( 6750\ \mathrm{rpm} \)
\( 1450\ \mathrm{rpm} \)
\( 107\ \mathrm{rpm} \)
quiz.solution: Using \( \omega_n=\sqrt{g/\delta}=\sqrt{9.81/1.96\times10^{-5}}=707\ \mathrm{rad/s} \), then converting: \( 707\times60/2\pi = 6750\ \mathrm{rpm} \). The 700 rpm answer reports the rad/s figure as though it were rpm, which is the standard trap in this calculation and worth a deliberate habit of checking. 1450 rpm is the operating speed, not a result, and 107 rpm would follow from dividing by \( 2\pi \) twice.

quiz.q: A shaft calculation returns a fatigue margin of 1.6 against a target of 2.0. Which change buys the most fatigue strength for the least cost?
choices: Switch to a higher-strength steel of the same grade family
Increase the fillet radius at the critical shoulder and grind that section
Shorten the bearing span
Increase the factor of safety in the calculation
quiz.solution: The critical section is governed by \( K_f \) and by surface finish, so a generous fillet radius plus a ground finish attacks both at once — Lesson 3 measured grinding alone at about 11% on \( S_e \), for one extra operation. A higher-strength steel raises \( S_{ut} \) but its rougher-surface and size knockdowns scale too, so the net gain in \( S_e \) is much smaller than the datasheet suggests. Shortening the span helps stiffness and moment but is usually fixed by the machine layout. Raising \( n \) in the calculation changes the requirement, not the shaft.

quiz.q: Why is the critical section for a shaft not always the section of maximum bending moment?
choices: Because the maximum moment is hard to locate accurately
Because a shoulder or keyway elsewhere can carry a high enough \( K_f \) to outweigh its smaller nominal moment
Because torque is constant along the shaft
Because bending moment does not affect fatigue
quiz.solution: What governs is the product of the nominal stress and the concentration factor at each candidate section. A keyway with \( K_f \) above 2, sitting where the moment is 80% of peak, beats a smooth section at 100% of peak. This is why sizing a shaft means checking every discontinuity — shoulders, keyways, grooves, press-fit ends — rather than the single worst point on the bending-moment diagram. Torque being constant is true on a simple shaft but does not bear on where bending governs.

5.kuwait: Applied case — the shaft that was strong enough and still unusable. A cooling-water pump is re-rated to a higher duty and the shaft is re-sized properly: reversed bending in the amplitude term, steady torque in the mean term, a fatigue margin of two, a ground fillet at the critical shoulder. The calculation is sound and the shaft never cracks. What it does instead is chew through mechanical seals, three in the first year. The cause is not strength at all. The re-rate moved the pump away from its best efficiency point, which raised the radial load, and the larger deflection at the seal faces exceeded what the seal could track — a stiffness failure on a shaft whose stress calculation was faultless. The fix is a stiffer shaft, and stiffness scales with \( d^4 \) and with \( E \), so a stronger steel would have changed nothing; the diameter went up and the bearing span came down. The general lesson is the one the strength calculation cannot tell you: passing the fatigue check answers whether the shaft breaks, not whether the machine works.
5.recap:
• A rotating shaft under fixed transverse load sees fully reversed bending (\( \sigma_m=0 \)) but steady torque (\( \tau_a=0 \)) — the two loads enter the fatigue criterion through different terms.
  • DE-Goodman inverts to a diameter directly: \( d^3=\frac{16n}{\pi}\left[\frac{2K_fM_a}{S_e}+\frac{\sqrt3K_{fs}T_m}{S_{ut}}\right] \).
  • Size at the critical section, not the maximum-moment section — a shoulder or keyway with a high \( K_f \) often governs.
  • Diameter responds to the cube root: doubling the factor of safety costs only 26% more diameter, so fatigue margin on a shaft is cheap.
  • Strength is not enough. Check bearing slope (about 0.001 rad) and gear-mesh deflection — stiffness depends on \( d^4 \) and \( E \), so a stronger steel does not help.
  • Check first critical speed, \( \omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}=\sqrt{g/\delta} \), and keep the operating speed well below it.
  • When a shaft is marginal, a bigger fillet radius, a ground finish, or a relocated keyway usually buys more life per unit cost than extra diameter.

6.lecture:
§1 · The torque path, and why it needs its own component

Lesson 5 sized a shaft to carry 98.8 N·m. It did not say how the torque gets onto the shaft. A pulley or impeller bore is a clearance fit — it must be, or the machine could not be assembled — and a clearance fit transmits nothing. Something has to bridge the gap, and the cheapest something is a rectangular bar dropped into matching slots in both parts. That is a key.

The tangential force it carries follows from the torque and the shaft radius, \( F = T/(d/2) \). For the Lesson 5 shaft that is \( 98.8/0.020 = 4939\ \mathrm{N} \). Everything else in this lesson is that force divided by an area.

§2 · Two areas, two checks

Look at the diagram and the two failure modes separate cleanly. The key can shear along the plane where shaft meets hub, resisted by the full plan area \( w \times L \). Or it can be crushed on the faces that transmit the push — and only half the key's height is available on each side, so the bearing area is \( (h/2) \times L \).

Key relation — the two key checks

\[ \tau = \frac{F}{wL} \le \frac{0.5S_y}{n}, \qquad \sigma_b = \frac{F}{(h/2)L} \le \frac{S_y}{n}, \qquad F=\frac{2T}{d} \]

Dividing one capacity by the other, the allowables cancel — shear is permitted half of what bearing is, and bearing has half the area — leaving simply \( T_{bearing}/T_{shear} = h/w \). A square key (\( h=w \)) is equally strong in both. Any key flatter than it is wide is bearing-governed.

That single ratio removes most of the guesswork. Standard keys for shafts in this size range are rectangular and flatter than they are wide — 12 × 8 mm on a 40 mm shaft — so bearing governs and the shear check is a formality. It is still worth running: a key that has been shortened to clear an obstruction, or a soft key in a hard hub, can move the answer.

§3 · Keys are sized by the hub, not by the torque

Run the numbers for the Lesson 5 shaft and something surprising falls out. The bearing check needs only 7.3 mm of key length to carry the running torque at a factor of safety of two. The hub is 60 mm long, and the key is made the full length of the hub, as it always is. The fitted key is therefore about eight times stronger than the running duty requires.

This is not waste. A key must survive the worst transient the drive can deliver — a direct-on-line motor start, a seized impeller, a pump ingesting a solid — and those can be many times running torque. Sizing a key to running load would be a design error. The real design decision is a different one: the key is deliberately the weakest link. At yield the fitted key lets go at about 1630 N·m while the shaft itself does not yield until around 2610 N·m, so an overload shears a two-dinar key rather than twisting a shaft that has to be pulled, machined and re-fitted. Keys are a mechanical fuse, and that is a feature.

§4 · When a key is not enough

A key has one structural cost, and Lesson 5 already priced it: the keyway is a stress raiser in the shaft, typically \( K_f \ge 2 \) in bending, sitting exactly where the torque is applied. Three alternatives avoid it.

A spline cuts many teeth around the shaft, so torque is shared and no single slot dominates the concentration. Do not over-credit it: misalignment means the teeth do not load equally, and standard practice assumes only about a quarter of them carry. Even so, ten teeth on the same seat as our key give roughly 1070 N·m against the key's 816 — around 30% more, with a far gentler concentration and a self-centring torque path.

An interference fit transmits torque by friction alone, with no slot at all: \( T = \mu p \pi d^2 L/2 \). At a modest 40 MPa contact pressure the same 40 mm seat carries about 905 N·m. The catch is assembly — the joint needs heating, pressing, or hydraulic dilation — and it is not designed to be taken apart.

Retaining rings solve a different problem: they locate a component axially, and they carry thrust, not torque. Their fine print is the groove. The ring is rarely what fails; what fails is the groove wall shearing or the ring dishing out of a groove machined too shallow or with too generous a corner radius. Groove depth, width and corner radius are catalogue values, and they are structural dimensions, not conveniences.

Closing. Compute the tangential force once, then divide by two different areas. Expect bearing to govern, expect the hub length to set the key size, and expect the key to be the component you would rather lose.

What this lesson assumes

  • Torque and tangential force (Statics) — \( T = F r \), the conversion this whole lesson rests on.
  • Direct shear and bearing stress (Strength of Materials L1) — force over the area that resists it, with no bending involved.
  • Yield strength and the factor of safety (Lesson 1) — how an allowable stress is set.
  • Maximum-shear-stress theory (Lesson 2) — why the shear allowable is half the tensile allowable.
  • Stress concentration (Lessons 2 and 5) — the keyway's \( K_f \), which is the cost this lesson weighs alternatives against.

quiz.q:
Torque capacity of a fitted key

Problem. A 12 × 8 mm key, 60 mm long, drives a hub on the 40 mm shaft of Lesson 5. The key steel has \( S_y = 340\ \mathrm{MPa} \) and the design factor is \( n = 2 \). Take the shear allowable as \( 0.5S_y/n \) and the bearing allowable as \( S_y/n \). Find: the torque capacity in each mode, which governs, and how it compares with the 98.8 N·m running torque.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Allowables: \( \tau_{all}=0.5(340)/2=85 \), \( \sigma_{all}=340/2=170\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) Shear: \( F = wL\tau_{all} = (0.012)(0.060)(85\times10^6) = 61{,}200\ \mathrm{N} \), so \( T = F d/2 = 61{,}200(0.020) = 1224\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (3) Bearing: \( F = (h/2)L\sigma_{all} = (0.004)(0.060)(170\times10^6) = 40{,}800\ \mathrm{N} \), so \( T = 816\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (4) Bearing governs at 816 N·m, which is \( 816/98.8 = 8.3 \) times the running torque.

Answer: 1224 N·m in shear, 816 N·m in bearing; bearing governs at 816 N·m, 8.3× the running duty. Sanity check: the ratio of the two capacities is \( 816/1224 = 0.667 \), which is exactly \( h/w = 8/12 \) as the general result predicts — the allowables and the length cancel. That agreement is worth checking on every key: if the computed ratio is not \( h/w \), an area or an allowable has been entered wrongly.

quiz.q:
How much key the torque actually needs

Problem. Same key section and material, same 40 mm shaft and 98.8 N·m running torque, same \( n = 2 \). Find: the minimum key length required by each check, and comment on the 60 mm length actually fitted.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( F = 2T/d = 2(98.8)/0.040 = 4939\ \mathrm{N} \). (2) Shear: \( L = F/(w\tau_{all}) = 4939/\big((0.012)(85\times10^6)\big) = 4.84\ \mathrm{mm} \). (3) Bearing: \( L = F/\big((h/2)\sigma_{all}\big) = 4939/\big((0.004)(170\times10^6)\big) = 7.26\ \mathrm{mm} \). (4) Bearing governs; 7.3 mm is required and 60 mm is fitted, a factor of 8.3.

Answer: 4.8 mm by shear, 7.3 mm by bearing; the fitted 60 mm is 8.3× the requirement. Sanity check: this is the same 8.3 factor as the previous problem, as it must be — capacity is linear in length, so the ratio of lengths and the ratio of torques are the same number computed two ways. The engineering point is that the key was never sized by this calculation: the hub length set it, and the calculation only confirms the transient capacity that surplus provides.

quiz.q:
Which one is the fuse?

Problem. Compare the ultimate torque paths at \( n = 1 \). The 12 × 8 × 60 mm key has \( S_y = 340\ \mathrm{MPa} \); the 40 mm shaft has \( S_y = 415\ \mathrm{MPa} \), and yields in torsion when \( \tau = 0.5S_y \), with polar section modulus \( \pi d^3/16 \). Find: the torque at which each yields, and say which gives way first.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Key, bearing mode at \( n=1 \): \( F = (0.004)(0.060)(340\times10^6) = 81{,}600\ \mathrm{N} \), so \( T = 81{,}600(0.020) = 1632\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (2) Shaft: \( \pi d^3/16 = \pi(0.040)^3/16 = 1.2566\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3} \), and \( \tau_y = 0.5(415) = 207.5\ \mathrm{MPa} \), so \( T = (207.5\times10^6)(1.2566\times10^{-5}) = 2608\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (3) Ratio \( 1632/2608 = 0.63 \).

Answer: key at 1632 N·m, shaft at 2608 N·m — the key yields first, at 63% of the shaft's torque. Sanity check: a 37% margin between fuse and protected part is comfortable but not extravagant, which is about right — too small and normal scatter lets the shaft go first, too large and the key shears during ordinary transients. Note that hardening the key to \( S_y = 560\ \mathrm{MPa} \) would put its capacity at 2688 N·m, above the shaft's, and silently transfer every future overload into the shaft.

quiz.q: For a key of width \( w \) and height \( h \), the ratio of bearing capacity to shear capacity is
choices: always 1
quiz.solution: Bearing capacity uses area \( (h/2)L \) with allowable \( S_y/n \); shear uses \( wL \) with allowable \( 0.5S_y/n \). The factor of two in the area and the factor of two in the allowable cancel exactly, leaving \( h/w \). The consequence is clean: a square key is balanced, and any key flatter than it is wide — which is the standard proportion — is bearing-governed. The \( h/(2w) \) answer forgets that the shear allowable is itself halved.

quiz.q: A 12 × 8 mm key 60 mm long carries 816 N·m while the running torque is 98.8 N·m. This eightfold surplus is
choices: a design error — the key should be shortened
intended: the key length is set by the hub, and the surplus covers start and stall transients while keeping the key as the weakest link
evidence the shaft is undersized
irrelevant, since keys are not load-bearing
quiz.solution: Keys are made the length of the hub as a matter of course, so the strength that results is an outcome rather than a target. The surplus is doing real work: a direct-on-line start or a jam can deliver several times running torque, and the key must survive those. It is also deliberately capped — at yield the key lets go before the shaft does, so an overload costs a key rather than a shaft. Shortening the key to the 7.3 mm the running torque needs would remove the transient capacity entirely.

quiz.q: The main structural argument for a spline over a single key is that
choices: splines are always cheaper to manufacture
torque is shared over many teeth and no single deep slot dominates the shaft's stress concentration
splines need no lubrication
splines eliminate the tangential force entirely
quiz.solution: A keyway is a single deep notch at the point of torque transfer, typically carrying \( K_f \ge 2 \) in bending. Spreading the same torque over many shallow teeth both raises capacity and, more importantly, gentles the concentration, while centring the torque path. Splines are generally more expensive to cut, not less, which is why keys remain the default. The tangential force is set by torque and radius and does not go anywhere.

quiz.q: Standard practice assumes only about 25% of a spline's teeth carry load because
choices: the other teeth are undersized by design
manufacturing tolerance and misalignment prevent all teeth from sharing equally
splines are loaded in only one direction
the outer teeth are outside the torque path
quiz.solution: Perfect load sharing would need every tooth flank on both parts to contact simultaneously, which no achievable tolerance delivers; small pitch and alignment errors concentrate the load on a minority of teeth. The 25% figure is a design allowance for that reality, not a statement about the teeth themselves — all of them are the same size and all lie in the torque path. This is why a spline's advantage over a key is a useful 30% or so, not the several-fold gain a naive tooth count would suggest.

quiz.q: An interference fit transmits torque by
choices: shear in a bridging component
friction at the contact pressure between shaft and hub
bearing on a machined flat
elastic bending of the hub
quiz.solution: There is no bridging component at all — that is the point. Pressing an oversized shaft into an undersized bore develops a contact pressure \( p \), and friction over the contact area carries the torque: \( T = \mu p \pi d^2 L/2 \). The shaft is left unslotted, so the keyway concentration disappears. The price is assembly: the joint must be heated, pressed or hydraulically dilated, and it is not intended to come apart again.

quiz.q: A retaining ring in a shaft groove is loaded primarily in
choices: torsion
axial thrust
bending about the shaft axis
shear from the key
quiz.solution: Retaining rings locate components axially and react the thrust that tries to push them off — they have no role in the torque path, which is the key's or the spline's job. The failure to watch for is not usually the ring: it is the groove, whose wall can shear or whose too-shallow depth or over-generous corner radius lets the ring dish and climb out under load. Groove depth, width and corner radius are catalogue values and should be treated as structural dimensions.

quiz.q: A drive shears its key twice a year on jams. A team replaces it with a much harder key and the shearing stops. The most likely consequence is
choices: the problem is solved at no cost
the next overload damages the shaft or hub instead, at far greater cost
the running torque increases
the keyway stress concentration disappears
quiz.solution: Hardening the key does not remove the overload; it moves the weakest link. Once the key's capacity exceeds the shaft's torsional yield, the next jam twists the shaft through its keyway — a repair measured in days against the key's hour. The correct responses are to address why the drive jams or to fit a torque limiter designed for the duty. Note the general habit this teaches: changing any component's material is a decision about which component fails first, and that question is worth asking explicitly.

quiz.q: A 40 mm shaft transmits 98.8 N·m. The tangential force the key must carry is
quiz.solution: The force acts at the shaft surface, one radius from the axis, so \( F = T/(d/2) = 2T/d = 2(98.8)/0.040 = 4939\ \mathrm{N} \). The 2470 N answer divides by the diameter instead of the radius — the single most common slip in this calculation, and it halves every stress that follows. The 9878 N figure multiplies by the diameter's reciprocal twice over, and 3.95 N confuses a torque with a force outright.

6.kuwait: Applied case — the upgrade that removed the fuse. A conveyor drive shears its drive key roughly twice a year, always on a jam. Each event costs two hours: back the drive off, drift out the remains of the key, fit a new one, restart. A maintenance team decides to end the nuisance by fitting keys cut from a much harder alloy steel. The shearing stops immediately. Nine months later the drive shaft twists through its keyway during a jam, and the repair takes eleven days — shaft removal, a replacement machined to order, re-alignment of the whole drive train. The original key was not a defect; it was the cheapest component in the torque path, deliberately sized to yield around 1630 N·m against a shaft that holds to roughly 2610 N·m, so that an overload destroyed something a fitter could replace in an hour. Hardening the key moved the weakest link into the shaft. The correct response to twice-yearly key failures was to ask why the conveyor jams twice a year, or to fit a proper torque limiter — not to strengthen the fuse. Any change to a component's material is a change to which component fails first, and that question should be asked before the order is placed.
6.recap:
• Torque reaches a clearance-fitted hub through a key; everything else follows from the tangential force \( F = 2T/d \).
  • Two checks, same force, different areas: shear over \( wL \) along the interface, bearing over \( (h/2)L \) on the driving faces.
  • The capacities divide down to \( T_{bearing}/T_{shear} = h/w \) — bearing governs for any key flatter than it is wide, and the two are equal for a square key.
  • Key length is set by the hub, not by the torque: the Lesson 5 duty needs 7.3 mm and gets 60 mm, about eight times the strength requirement.
  • That surplus is intentional. Keys must survive start and stall transients, and the key is designed as the mechanical fuse — yielding near 1630 N·m against the shaft's 2610 N·m.
  • A keyway costs \( K_f \ge 2 \) in the shaft. Splines (about 1070 N·m here, only ~25% of teeth assumed loaded) and interference fits (\( T=\mu p\pi d^2L/2 \), about 905 N·m) avoid the slot.
  • Retaining rings carry thrust, not torque, and their groove dimensions — depth, width, corner radius — are structural, not cosmetic.

7.lecture:
§1 · What the manufacturing course established, and what it left

Manufacturing Processes II settled how preload is achieved: torque is only a proxy, the nut factor \( K \) is an assumption rather than a constant, and the same torque on a lubricated bolt delivers substantially more preload than on a dry one. Take all of that as given here. This lesson answers the design question underneath it — why the joint wants preload at all, and how much.

The naive picture is that a bolt holds a joint the way a hook holds a bucket: apply 20 kN to the joint and the bolt carries 20 kN. That picture is wrong, and the extent to which it is wrong is the most useful number in fastener design.

§2 · Two springs, and the load-sharing constant

Tightening a bolt stretches it and compresses the members it clamps. Both are elastic, so both are springs, and they are loaded in opposition: an external load that stretches the bolt further simultaneously lets the members expand back toward their free length. The two share the load in proportion to their stiffnesses.

Key relation — load sharing in a preloaded joint

\[ C=\frac{k_b}{k_b+k_m}, \qquad F_b=F_i+CP, \qquad F_m=F_i-(1-C)P \]

\( C \) is the fraction of an external load \( P \) that reaches the bolt. Since \( F_b - F_m = P \) always, the two expressions are one statement: whatever the members stop carrying, the bolt picks up.

For an M12 bolt through a 40 mm steel grip, \( k_b \approx 436 \) and \( k_m \approx 2361\ \mathrm{MN/m} \), giving \( C = 0.156 \). A 20 kN external load raises bolt tension by 3.1 kN and reduces clamp force by 16.9 kN. The bolt barely notices. What the joint actually spends under load is not bolt strength — it is clamp force.

§3 · The two ways a preloaded joint fails

Because clamp force is the currency, the first failure mode is separation: when \( F_m \) reaches zero the members part, and from that instant the bolt carries the entire external load directly. Every protective property in the paragraph above vanishes at once. The separation load is \( P_0 = F_i/(1-C) \), which for the worked joint is 44.9 kN against an applied 20 kN — a margin of 2.25.

The second is bolt yielding, checked against the proof strength: \( n = (S_pA_t-F_i)/(CP) \), here 4.05. Note which of the two governs. The bolt is the strong part of this joint by a wide margin; separation arrives first, and a designer worrying about bolt strength while ignoring clamp force is watching the wrong number. Preload is normally set at about 75% of proof load for a reusable connection precisely to push separation as far away as possible without yielding the bolt on assembly.

§4 · Fatigue, and why preload is the cheapest fix available

Fluctuating loads are where the stiffness ratio pays for itself. For a load cycling between zero and \( P \), the bolt's stress amplitude is \( \sigma_a = CP/2A_t \) — the external amplitude scaled by \( C \). In the worked joint that is 18.5 MPa. Remove the preload and the bolt would see \( P/2A_t = 118.7\ \mathrm{MPa} \) instead, larger by a factor of exactly \( 1/C = 6.4 \).

This is worth stating plainly, because it inverts an intuition. Tightening a bolt more makes it last longer under cyclic load. The mean stress rises, which Lesson 4 says is damaging, but the amplitude falls by far more, and fatigue answers to amplitude first. The overwhelming majority of fatigue failures in bolted joints are loose-joint failures.

The same reasoning explains why gaskets are treated with suspicion in dynamically loaded joints. A soft gasket collapses \( k_m \), which drives \( C \) up, which routes the external load into the bolt:

Joint construction\( C \)Bolt stress amplitude
Steel on steel0.15618.5 MPa
Gasketed, \( k_m/4 \)0.42550.4 MPa
Soft gasket, \( k_m/10 \)0.64977.0 MPa

A soft gasket has multiplied the bolt's fatigue loading fourfold without a single number in the load specification changing. This is the design fact behind a rule most plants enforce by habit: use the hardest, thinnest gasket the sealing duty permits, and never substitute a softer one because it seals more easily.

Closing. A preloaded joint is two springs in opposition, and \( C \) says how the load divides between them. Design for clamp force, check separation before bolt strength, and treat any change that softens the members as a change to the bolt's fatigue life.
7.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Torque–preload and the nut factor (Manufacturing Processes II L10) — \( T=KdF_i \) and why \( K \) is an assumption; this lesson takes preload as achieved and asks what it does.
  • Axial stiffness (Strength of Materials L1) — \( k=AE/L \), the model for the bolt spring.
  • Springs in parallel (Physics I) — two elements sharing a common deflection share load in proportion to stiffness.
  • Goodman criterion (Lesson 4) — the fatigue check applied to the bolt, with preload supplying a large mean stress.
  • Proof strength — the fastener-specific allowable, below yield, that grade markings are defined against.

Glossary

TermEquationWhen to use

Bolt stiffness\( k_b=A_tE/l \)Grip-length spring rate of the fastener.

quiz.q:
How an external load actually divides

Problem. An M12 × 1.75 grade 8.8 bolt (\( S_p=600\ \mathrm{MPa} \)) clamps a 40 mm grip of steel members. Take \( E=207\ \mathrm{GPa} \), \( k_b=A_tE/l \), and the Wileman member stiffness \( k_m=EdA e^{Bd/l} \) with \( A=0.78715 \), \( B=0.62873 \). The joint carries an external load of 20 kN per bolt, and preload is set at 75% of proof load. Find: \( A_t \), \( C \), the preload, and the bolt and member loads under the external load.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( A_t=\frac{\pi}{4}(12-0.9382\times1.75)^2 = \frac{\pi}{4}(10.358)^2 = 84.3\ \mathrm{mm^2} \). (2) \( k_b = (84.3\times10^{-6})(207\times10^9)/0.040 = 436\ \mathrm{MN/m} \). (3) \( k_m = (207\times10^9)(0.012)(0.78715)e^{0.62873(0.012)/0.040} = 1.955\times10^9 \times e^{0.1886} = 2361\ \mathrm{MN/m} \). (4) \( C = 436/(436+2361) = 0.156 \). (5) \( F_i = 0.75(84.3\times10^{-6})(600\times10^6) = 37{,}920\ \mathrm{N} \). (6) \( F_b = 37{,}920+0.156(20{,}000) = 41{,}038\ \mathrm{N} \); \( F_m = 37{,}920-0.844(20{,}000) = 21{,}038\ \mathrm{N} \).

Answer: \( A_t=84.3\ \mathrm{mm^2} \), \( C=0.156 \), \( F_i=37.9 \), \( F_b=41.0 \), \( F_m=21.0\ \mathrm{kN} \). Sanity check: \( F_b-F_m = 41{,}038-21{,}038 = 20{,}000\ \mathrm{N} \), exactly the applied load — the check that catches almost any arithmetic slip in this calculation. Note the physical result: a 20 kN load added 3.1 kN to the bolt and removed 16.9 kN of clamp force. The joint spends clamp force, not bolt strength.

quiz.q:
Which failure arrives first

Problem. For the same joint (\( C=0.156 \), \( F_i=37{,}920\ \mathrm{N} \), \( A_t=84.3\ \mathrm{mm^2} \), \( S_p=600\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( P=20\ \mathrm{kN} \)) find: the load at which the joint separates, the factor of safety against separation, and the factor of safety against bolt yielding. State which governs.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Separation when \( F_m=0 \): \( P_0 = F_i/(1-C) = 37{,}920/0.844 = 44{,}923\ \mathrm{N} \). (2) \( n_{sep} = P_0/P = 44{,}923/20{,}000 = 2.25 \). (3) Yielding when \( F_b = S_pA_t = (600\times10^6)(84.3\times10^{-6}) = 50{,}580\ \mathrm{N} \): \( n_{yield} = (50{,}580-37{,}920)/(0.156\times20{,}000) = 12{,}660/3{,}118 = 4.05 \).

Answer: \( P_0=44.9\ \mathrm{kN} \), \( n_{sep}=2.25 \), \( n_{yield}=4.05 \) — separation governs. Sanity check: the bolt is nearly twice as far from yielding as the joint is from opening, which is the normal state of a properly preloaded steel joint and the reason clamp force is the design variable. A useful cross-check on \( n_{sep} \): at \( P=P_0 \) the member load should compute to zero, and indeed \( 37{,}920-0.844(44{,}923)=0 \).

quiz.q:
What preload buys under cyclic load

Problem. The 20 kN external load on the same joint fluctuates between zero and its full value. Find: the bolt's stress amplitude, and the amplitude the same bolt would see if the joint were assembled with no effective preload so that the bolt carried the whole external load. Express the improvement as a ratio.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Preloaded: the bolt's share of the load range is \( CP = 0.156(20{,}000) = 3{,}118\ \mathrm{N} \), so the force amplitude is \( CP/2 = 1{,}559\ \mathrm{N} \) and \( \sigma_a = 1{,}559/(84.3\times10^{-6}) = 18.5\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (2) Unpreloaded: the bolt takes all of \( P \), so \( \sigma_a = 10{,}000/(84.3\times10^{-6}) = 118.7\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (3) Ratio \( 118.7/18.5 = 6.4 \).

Answer: 18.5 MPa preloaded against 118.7 MPa unpreloaded — a factor of 6.4. Sanity check: that ratio is exactly \( 1/C = 1/0.156 = 6.4 \), which it must be, since preload divides the bolt's share of the load range by \( C \) and changes nothing else about the amplitude. The counter-intuitive conclusion is sound: tightening the bolt raises its mean stress but cuts its amplitude sixfold, and fatigue answers to amplitude first. Loose joints, not overtightened ones, are what break bolts.

quiz.q: In a preloaded bolted joint, the stiffness constant \( C=k_b/(k_b+k_m) \) represents
choices: the fraction of the preload carried by the members
the fraction of an external load that reaches the bolt
the ratio of bolt stress to member stress
the efficiency of the torque–preload conversion
quiz.solution: \( C \) partitions the external load: the bolt takes \( CP \) and the members give up \( (1-C)P \) of clamp force. Preload itself is not divided by \( C \) — it is equal and opposite in the two elements by definition. The torque–preload conversion is governed by the nut factor \( K \), an entirely separate quantity covered in Manufacturing Processes II. Because members are typically several times stiffer than the bolt, \( C \) is usually small, around 0.1 to 0.2 for steel-on-steel.

quiz.q: A joint has \( F_i = 30\ \mathrm{kN} \) and \( C = 0.20 \). Under a 25 kN external load, the clamp force remaining between the members is
choices: \( 5\ \mathrm{kN} \)
\( 10\ \mathrm{kN} \)
\( 30\ \mathrm{kN} \)
\( 35\ \mathrm{kN} \)
quiz.solution: \( F_m = F_i - (1-C)P = 30 - 0.8(25) = 30 - 20 = 10\ \mathrm{kN} \). The 5 kN answer subtracts the full external load, which would be right only if the members were infinitely stiff. The bolt meanwhile rises to \( 30+0.2(25)=35\ \mathrm{kN} \) — that is the last option, the bolt load rather than the clamp force. Note how close this joint is to separating: 10 kN of clamp force left from 30, at only 25 kN of a load that would separate it at 37.5 kN.

quiz.q: Once an external load exceeds the separation load \( P_0 \),
choices: the bolt begins to carry the entire external load directly
the members carry the excess
the preload increases to compensate
the stiffness constant \( C \) falls toward zero
quiz.solution: Separation is the point at which clamp force reaches zero. Beyond it there is nothing for the members to give up, so the sharing mechanism ends and the bolt takes the whole load — with the fatigue amplitude jumping by the factor \( 1/C \) that preload had been buying. This is why separation, not bolt yield, is normally the governing check: crossing it does not merely reduce a margin, it removes the protective behaviour the joint was designed around.

quiz.q: Replacing a thin hard gasket with a thick soft one, all loads unchanged, will
choices: reduce the bolt's stress amplitude because the gasket absorbs the load
raise \( C \) and therefore raise the bolt's stress amplitude
leave the bolt's fatigue loading unchanged
raise the separation load
quiz.solution: A soft gasket lowers \( k_m \), and since \( C=k_b/(k_b+k_m) \), lowering \( k_m \) raises \( C \) — routing more of the external load into the bolt. Cutting \( k_m \) to a quarter takes \( C \) from 0.156 to 0.425 and the bolt's amplitude from 18.5 to 50.4 MPa. The gasket does not absorb load in any protective sense; it makes the joint's stiff element less stiff. Separation load also falls, since \( P_0=F_i/(1-C) \) shrinks as \( C \) grows.

quiz.q: The tensile stress area of an M12 × 1.75 bolt, from \( A_t=\frac{\pi}{4}(d-0.9382p)^2 \), is closest to
choices: \( 84\ \mathrm{mm^2} \)
\( 76\ \mathrm{mm^2} \)
\( 96\ \mathrm{mm^2} \)
quiz.solution: \( 12-0.9382(1.75)=10.358\ \mathrm{mm} \), and \( \frac{\pi}{4}(10.358)^2=84.3\ \mathrm{mm^2} \). The 113 mm² answer is the area of the full 12 mm shank, which overstates capacity by a third — threads remove real material and the stress area exists precisely to account for that. Using the minor diameter alone would give about 76 mm², slightly conservative; the standard formula sits between the two because the failure surface runs through neither extreme exactly.

quiz.q: Preload for a reusable connection is commonly specified as \( 0.75A_tS_p \) rather than a smaller fraction because
choices: it makes the bolt easier to remove
high preload pushes the separation load up and cuts the bolt's fatigue amplitude, while staying below proof on assembly
it compensates for an unknown nut factor
lower preloads would yield the members
quiz.solution: Both benefits scale with preload. Separation load is \( F_i/(1-C) \), so more preload directly buys more margin before the joint opens, and staying clamped is what keeps the bolt's fatigue amplitude at \( CP/2A_t \) rather than the far larger unpreloaded value. The 0.75 factor is where those gains stop before assembly stress reaches proof. It does not compensate for nut-factor uncertainty — that scatter is exactly why the remaining 25% margin is needed.

quiz.q: A bolt in a dynamically loaded joint keeps failing in fatigue at the first engaged thread. Of the following, the change most likely to help is
choices: reducing the assembly torque so the bolt carries less mean stress
restoring or increasing preload, and stiffening the members
fitting a softer gasket to cushion the load
using a longer bolt of the same grade
quiz.solution: Fatigue answers to amplitude, and amplitude is \( CP/2A_t \) — reduced by keeping the joint clamped and by anything that lowers \( C \), which means stiffer members. Reducing torque moves the joint toward separation and can increase the amplitude several-fold; it is the intuitive answer and the wrong one. A softer gasket raises \( C \) and makes matters worse. A longer bolt lowers \( k_b \) and so lowers \( C \) slightly, which is a genuine if modest help — but it is second-order beside simply having the joint properly tight.

quiz.q: Two joints carry the same external load. Joint A has \( C=0.15 \); joint B, identical but with a much less stiff member stack, has \( C=0.60 \). Compared with A, the bolt in B experiences
choices: four times the stress amplitude
the same stress amplitude
one quarter the stress amplitude
no cyclic stress at all
quiz.solution: Amplitude scales directly with \( C \), so \( 0.60/0.15 = 4 \). The whole of a preloaded joint's fatigue advantage lives in keeping \( C \) small, which means keeping the members far stiffer than the bolt. It is worth noticing that nothing about the bolt itself changed between the two joints — same grade, same size, same load — and its fatigue duty still quadrupled. Joint stiffness is a design variable, not a detail.

7.kuwait: Applied case — the gasket substitution that broke the bolts. A pump discharge flange has sealed without complaint for years on a thin, hard gasket. During a shutdown the specified gasket is unavailable and a softer, thicker one is fitted instead — it seals immediately, at lower torque, and everyone regards this as an improvement. Within four months bolts begin failing one at a time, always fracturing at the first engaged thread, always with the beach marks of fatigue rather than the cup-and-cone of overload. Nothing about the process changed: same pressure, same pump, same pulsation from the same reciprocating source. What changed was \( k_m \). The softer gasket cut member stiffness roughly fourfold, which raised \( C \) from about 0.16 to about 0.43, which raised the bolts' stress amplitude from roughly 18 to roughly 50 MPa — a load the bolts had never seen and were never selected for. The lower torque made it worse, since less preload meant a lower separation load as well. The repair was to return to the specified gasket, not to upgrade the bolts. The transferable point is that a gasket is a structural member of the joint, and substituting one is a stiffness change that silently re-rates every bolt around it.
7.recap:
• A preloaded joint is two springs in opposition: the bolt stretches, the members are compressed, and an external load is shared between them.
  • \( C=k_b/(k_b+k_m) \) is the fraction of external load reaching the bolt. For M12 through a 40 mm steel grip, \( C=0.156 \) — a 20 kN load raises bolt tension by only 3.1 kN.
  • \( F_b=F_i+CP \) and \( F_m=F_i-(1-C)P \), and always \( F_b-F_m=P \).
  • Separation at \( P_0=F_i/(1-C) \) is usually the governing failure, not bolt yield — here 2.25 against 4.05. Design for clamp force.
  • Preload is normally \( 0.75A_tS_p \) for reusable joints; the tensile stress area follows from \( A_t=\frac{\pi}{4}(d-0.9382p)^2 \).
  • Under cyclic load the bolt's amplitude is \( CP/2A_t \) — smaller than an unpreloaded bolt's by exactly \( 1/C \), here 6.4×. Tightening a bolt properly makes it last longer.
  • Softening the members raises \( C \). A gasket at \( k_m/4 \) takes the bolt's stress amplitude from 18.5 to 50.4 MPa with no change to the applied load.

8.lecture:
§1 · The throat, and why leg size is not the strength

A fillet weld is drawn and specified by its leg length \( h \), the size measured along either fused face. It does not fail there. The failure plane is the throat, the shortest path across the weld, and for the standard equal-leg fillet that path is \( t = h\cos45° = 0.707h \).

Everything follows from that. A 6 mm fillet has 4.24 mm of resisting thickness, not 6 — specify a weld by its leg and calculate it by its throat, and never confuse the two. It also explains why doubling a fillet's leg doubles its cost in deposited metal roughly fourfold while doubling its strength only twofold: weld volume goes as \( h^2 \), strength as \( h \). Long, small fillets are almost always cheaper than short, large ones for the same capacity.

Key relation — fillet weld capacity

\[ \tau=\frac{F}{0.707\,h\,L}, \qquad \tau\le\tau_{all} \]

Fillet welds are always checked in shear on the throat, whatever direction the load comes from — a transversely loaded fillet is stronger than a longitudinally loaded one, but design practice conservatively treats them alike.

§2 · Weld groups behave exactly like bolt groups

An eccentric load on a weld group is the same problem as an eccentric load on a bolt group, and the same method solves it. Reduce the load at the centroid to a force plus a couple; the force produces a uniform direct shear over the whole weld, and the couple produces a torsional shear proportional to distance from the centroid. Add the two as vectors at each candidate point, and the largest resultant governs.

The one convenience welds allow is the unit-throat trick. Since throat thickness is constant and unknown at the start, treat the welds as lines of unit thickness, compute the group's properties per unit throat, get a result in force per unit length, and divide by the allowable stress at the end to obtain the throat required. The algebra stays linear and the throat never has to be guessed.

Key relation — eccentric weld group, unit throat

\[ \tau'=\frac{P}{A_w}, \qquad \tau''=\frac{Tr}{J_u}, \qquad J_u=I_x+I_y, \qquad R=|\vec\tau'+\vec\tau''| \]

\( A_w \) is total weld length, \( J_u \) the polar second moment of the weld lines about the group centroid, and \( r \) the distance to the point being checked. Required throat is \( t=R/\tau_{all} \).

Two habits matter. Take the components of \( \tau'' \) rather than its magnitude — the resultant depends on the angle between the two shears, and adding magnitudes overstates the answer at some corners and understates it at others. And check every corner: on an asymmetric group the worst point is not always the farthest one, because the direct shear may oppose the torsional shear there.

§3 · Where welds crack

Welds fail in fatigue at the toe — the line where the weld metal meets the parent plate. Three things meet at that line and all of them are unhelpful. The geometry changes abruptly, so there is a stress concentration. The weld's own cooling contraction leaves a tensile residual stress there, often near yield. And the toe is where slag inclusions and undercut end up, so it is where the sharpest defects are.

The consequence is a fact that surprises people the first time: the fatigue strength of a welded detail is essentially independent of the parent steel's strength. Specifying a higher-grade steel raises the static capacity and does nothing whatever for the fatigue life of the weld, because the crack starts in a residual-stress field at a geometric notch that the material upgrade has not changed. Fatigue of welded structures is therefore classified by detail geometry — a category number giving the stress range the detail survives at two million cycles — not by material.

§4 · Designing for weld fatigue

Those categories run on a law of the form \( \Delta\sigma^3 N = \text{constant} \), and the cube is the whole story. A detail good for 80 MPa of stress range at two million cycles survives about 4.7 million cycles at 60 MPa, and only about 1.02 million at 100 MPa. A 25% increase in stress range costs half the life.

Design follows directly. Reduce the stress range at the toe rather than raising strength anywhere: use a better detail category — a full-penetration butt weld ground flush is in a different class from a fillet-welded lap — put the weld where the stress is low, avoid stopping and starting welds at highly stressed points, and grind or peen the toe when a detail cannot be improved. All of these change the geometry, which is the only variable weld fatigue actually responds to.

Closing. Specify by leg, calculate on throat. Treat a weld group exactly like a bolt group and add the two shears as vectors. Then design the fatigue case around detail geometry and stress range, because the steel grade will not help.

quiz.q:
An eccentrically loaded weld group

Problem. A bracket is attached to a column by two vertical fillet welds, each 150 mm long and 100 mm apart. A vertical load of 20 kN acts 200 mm out from the weld group's centroid. Using the unit-throat method, find: \( A_w \), \( J_u \), the direct and torsional shears, and the resultant at the critical corner.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( A_w = 2(150) = 300\ \mathrm{mm} \). (2) \( I_x = 2(150)^3/12 = 562{,}500 \); \( I_y = 2(150)(50)^2 = 750{,}000 \); \( J_u = 1{,}312{,}500\ \mathrm{mm^3} \). (3) Direct: \( \tau' = 20{,}000/300 = 66.7\ \mathrm{N/mm} \), acting downward. (4) \( T = 20{,}000(200) = 4\times10^6\ \mathrm{N\,mm} \). At the corner \( (x,y)=(50,75) \): \( \tau''_x = Ty/J_u = 228.6 \), \( \tau''_y = Tx/J_u = 152.4\ \mathrm{N/mm} \). (5) At the bottom-right corner the torsional and direct vertical parts add: \( R_x = 228.6 \), \( R_y = 152.4+66.7 = 219.1 \), so \( R = \sqrt{228.6^2+219.1^2} = 316.6\ \mathrm{N/mm} \).

Answer: \( A_w=300\ \mathrm{mm} \), \( J_u=1.3125\times10^6\ \mathrm{mm^3} \), \( R=316.6\ \mathrm{N/mm} \). Sanity check: the resultant is 4.75 times the direct shear alone, which is the measure of how much the eccentricity costs. Note also that adding the magnitudes \( 66.7+274.7=341.4 \) would overstate the answer by 8% — the two shears are not parallel, and components are not optional.

quiz.q:
From resultant to a drawing callout

Problem. The weld group above carries \( R = 316.6\ \mathrm{N/mm} \) at unit throat. The allowable shear stress on the weld metal is 145 MPa. Find: the required throat and leg size, and the factor of safety if a 6 mm fillet is specified instead.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( t = R/\tau_{all} = 316.6/145 = 2.18\ \mathrm{mm} \). (2) \( h = t/0.707 = 3.09\ \mathrm{mm} \). (3) A 6 mm fillet gives \( t = 0.707(6) = 4.24\ \mathrm{mm} \), so the stress is \( 316.6/4.24 = 74.6\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (4) \( n = 145/74.6 = 1.94 \).

Answer: 2.18 mm throat, 3.09 mm leg required; a 6 mm fillet gives \( n = 1.94 \). Sanity check: strength called for about 3 mm, and 6 mm was specified — not waste, but the minimum fillet size that plate thickness and process control permit. This is the normal outcome for bracket welds and worth recognising: like the key in Lesson 6, the weld is usually sized by something other than the load it carries.

quiz.q:
The cube law in practice

Problem. A welded detail is classified at 80 MPa stress range at \( 2\times10^6 \) cycles, on the law \( \Delta\sigma^3N = \) constant. Find: the constant, the life at 100 MPa and at 60 MPa, and comment on what a 25% reduction in stress range is worth.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( C = 80^3(2\times10^6) = 1.024\times10^{12} \). (2) At 100 MPa: \( N = 1.024\times10^{12}/100^3 = 1.02\times10^6 \) cycles. (3) At 60 MPa: \( N = 1.024\times10^{12}/60^3 = 4.74\times10^6 \) cycles. (4) Going from 80 to 60 MPa — a 25% reduction — multiplies life by \( (80/60)^3 = 2.37 \).

Answer: \( C=1.024\times10^{12} \); 1.02 million cycles at 100 MPa and 4.74 million at 60 MPa. A 25% cut in range is worth about 2.4× the life. Sanity check: the relation is symmetric and brutal in both directions — raising the range from 80 to 100 MPa leaves \( (80/100)^3 = 0.512 \), almost exactly half the life. Any change that quietly increases stress range at a weld toe by a quarter has halved the structure's fatigue life, which is why bracing and detail changes outperform material changes so decisively here.

quiz.q: A fillet weld is specified with a 10 mm leg. The thickness that actually resists the load is
choices: \( 10\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 7.07\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 14.1\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 5\ \mathrm{mm} \)
quiz.solution: Failure runs across the throat, the shortest path through the weld, which for an equal-leg fillet is \( 0.707h = 7.07\ \mathrm{mm} \). Designing on the 10 mm leg would overstate capacity by 41%. The 14.1 mm figure is the hypotenuse across the two legs, which is the longest path rather than the shortest, and 5 mm confuses the throat with half the leg. Specify by leg, calculate on throat.

quiz.q: In the unit-throat method for weld groups, the welds are treated as lines because
choices: weld throat is negligible compared with the group size
the throat is the unknown being solved for, so keeping it out of the group properties leaves a linear problem
torsional shear does not depend on thickness
line welds are stronger than area welds
quiz.solution: At the start of the calculation the throat is precisely what is not yet known. Computing \( A_w \) and \( J_u \) at unit thickness gives a resultant in force per unit length, and dividing by the allowable stress at the end returns the throat directly — no iteration and no guessed starting size. The throat is not negligible, and thickness certainly does affect the stress; it is simply factored out of the geometry and restored at the last step.

quiz.q: When combining direct and torsional shear on a weld group, using the magnitudes \( \tau'+\tau'' \) rather than vector components
choices: is exact, since both are shear stresses
is wrong in general, because the two act in different directions and their resultant depends on the angle between them
is conservative at every point on the group
is only valid for symmetric groups
quiz.solution: The two shears are vectors with different directions at every point, so the resultant follows from components. On the worked bracket, adding magnitudes gives 341.4 against the correct 316.6 N/mm — 8% high at that corner. It is not reliably conservative either: at a corner where the torsional component opposes the direct shear, the true resultant is smaller still, and at some geometries the worst point is not the farthest one at all. Symmetry does not rescue the shortcut.

quiz.q: Fatigue cracks in welded joints characteristically start at the weld toe because
choices: the weld metal is weaker than the parent plate there
a geometric notch, near-yield tensile residual stress, and the worst defects all coincide at that line
the throat is thinnest at the toe
the toe cools last and stays hottest
quiz.solution: Three unfavourable things meet at the toe: an abrupt change of section that concentrates stress, a tensile residual stress left by the weld's own contraction that is often close to yield, and the undercut and slag that tend to end up exactly there. Weld metal is normally overmatched — stronger than the parent plate — so material weakness is not the explanation. The throat is a plane through the weld, not a feature of the toe.

quiz.q: Specifying a higher-strength parent steel for a fillet-welded detail loaded in fatigue will
choices: proportionally increase the fatigue life
leave the fatigue life essentially unchanged, because weld-toe fatigue depends on detail geometry and stress range rather than material strength
reduce the fatigue life
increase the fatigue life only above two million cycles
quiz.solution: The crack initiates at a geometric notch inside a near-yield residual stress field, and a stronger steel changes neither. This is why welded structures are classified by detail category — a number describing the joint's geometry — and why the design curves carry no material term at all. The practical consequence is that the useful interventions are geometric: a better detail, a ground toe, a weld relocated to lower stress, or a reduced stress range.

quiz.q: A welded detail's stress range is reduced from 100 MPa to 80 MPa. On \( \Delta\sigma^3N=\text{const} \), the life is multiplied by about
quiz.solution: \( (100/80)^3 = 1.953 \) — a 20% cut in stress range nearly doubles the life. The 1.25 answer treats the law as linear, which badly undersells what detailing work is worth. The 0.51 figure is the same cube applied the wrong way round, and is what happens if the range goes up from 80 to 100. The cube is the reason small reductions in stress range are the most cost-effective intervention available on a fatigue-limited welded structure.

quiz.q: A 200 mm run of 8 mm fillet weld carries a concentric load. With an allowable shear stress of 145 MPa, its capacity is closest to
choices: \( 232\ \mathrm{kN} \)
\( 164\ \mathrm{kN} \)
\( 116\ \mathrm{kN} \)
\( 82\ \mathrm{kN} \)
quiz.solution: The throat is \( 0.707(8) = 5.66\ \mathrm{mm} \), so the resisting area is \( 5.66\times200 = 1131\ \mathrm{mm^2} \) and the capacity is \( 1131(145) = 164\ \mathrm{kN} \). The 232 kN answer uses the 8 mm leg as the resisting thickness — the standard error, and 41% unconservative. Halving to 82 kN would follow from taking the throat as half the leg rather than \( 0.707 \) of it. Note the useful shortcut this suggests: an 8 mm fillet is worth about 0.82 kN per millimetre of run at this allowable.

quiz.q: Two designs carry the same load with the same total weld capacity: design A uses a short 12 mm fillet, design B a longer 6 mm fillet. Design B generally
choices: costs more, because it needs more weld length
costs less, because deposited volume goes as the square of leg size while strength goes only as the first power
is weaker, because small fillets cannot be relied upon
is identical in cost and strength
quiz.solution: Strength is proportional to \( 0.707hL \) — linear in leg size — while the cross-sectional area of deposited metal goes as \( h^2/2 \). Halving the leg and doubling the length therefore holds capacity constant while roughly halving the metal deposited, along with the heat input and distortion that come with it. This is why weld callouts favour long small fillets, subject to the minimum size the plate thickness requires and to fitting the weld into the space available.

8.kuwait: Applied case — the bracket that was upgraded into failure. A pipe-support bracket fillet-welded to a structural column develops cracks in its welds after about two years of service under a pulsating line. The repair specification calls for the bracket to be remade from a higher-grade steel, on the reasoning that a stronger bracket will last longer. It cracks again in fourteen months, in the same place — along the weld toe. Nothing had been done about the actual mechanism. Weld-toe fatigue is governed by the detail's geometry and the stress range at the toe, and both were unchanged; the upgraded plate raised static capacity and left the residual stress field, the notch at the toe, and the applied stress range exactly as they were. The successful repair was geometric: the attachment was extended so the weld ended in a region of lower stress, the toe was ground to a smooth radius, and the support was re-braced to cut the stress range by roughly a quarter — which, on a cube law, is worth about double the life on its own. The general lesson is worth carrying into any review: when a crack is at a weld toe, the question is never which steel, it is which detail and how large a stress range.
8.recap:
• Fillet welds are specified by leg \( h \) but fail on the throat \( t=0.707h \) — a 6 mm fillet resists on 4.24 mm.
  • Weld volume grows as \( h^2 \) while strength grows as \( h \), so long small fillets beat short large ones for the same capacity.
  • An eccentric load on a weld group is solved exactly like a bolt group: direct shear \( P/A_w \) plus torsional shear \( Tr/J_u \), added as vectors at each corner.
  • Use the unit-throat method — treat welds as lines, work in force per unit length, and divide by the allowable at the end to get the throat.
  • On the worked bracket, eccentricity took 66.7 N/mm of direct shear to a resultant of 316.6 N/mm — a factor of 4.75 from the moment alone.
  • Welds crack at the toe, where a geometric notch, near-yield tensile residual stress, and the worst defects coincide.
  • Weld fatigue strength is essentially independent of the parent steel's grade; details are classified by geometry, on \( \Delta\sigma^3N=\text{const} \).
  • The cube law is severe: 80 → 100 MPa of stress range halves the life. Improve the detail or cut the range; do not upgrade the steel.

9.lecture:
§1 · A spring is a torsion bar wound up

Push down on a helical compression spring and the wire does not bend in any useful sense — it twists. Cut the wire anywhere and the internal action is almost entirely a torque \( T=FD/2 \), the axial force acting at the mean coil radius. That single observation gives the whole component, because the torsion of a round bar is already known from Strength of Materials.

Two corrections separate the real spring from that idealisation. The applied force also produces a direct transverse shear across the wire, and because the coil is curved, the material on the inside of the coil is shorter and carries more of the twist than the outside. Both effects raise stress on the inner fibre, and both are collected into a single multiplier.

Key relation — spring stress and the Wahl factor

\[ \tau = K_W\frac{8FD}{\pi d^3}, \qquad K_W = \frac{4C-1}{4C-4}+\frac{0.615}{C}, \qquad C=\frac{D}{d} \]

\( C \) is the spring index. At \( C=7.5 \), \( K_W = 1.197 \) — the inner fibre carries 20% more stress than the plain torsion formula predicts, and it is where every spring fails.

The spring index is worth reading as a manufacturability number as well as a stress one. Below about 4 the coil is so tightly wound that \( K_W \) climbs steeply and the wire is hard to form; above about 12 the spring is floppy and tangles in handling. Designs live between, and \( C \) between 6 and 9 is comfortable.

§2 · Rate, and how violently it responds to wire size

Deflection accumulates twist over the whole developed length of the wire, which gives the rate directly.

Key relation — spring rate

\[ k=\frac{Gd^4}{8D^3N_a} \]

\( N_a \) is the number of active coils — the total less the dead coils at each end. Note the exponents: rate goes as the fourth power of wire diameter and the inverse cube of coil diameter.

Those exponents dominate spring design in practice. Changing the wire from 4.0 to 3.5 mm — a 12.5% reduction that no drawing reader would call significant — takes the rate from 9.40 to 5.51 N/mm, a loss of 41%. Wire diameter is not a tolerance-band decision; it is the design. It is also why a spring that has been substituted "like for like" from a bin of similar-looking parts is a real hazard on a machine whose behaviour depends on a specific rate.

§3 · The two checks that are not stress

A spring can pass its stress calculation and still be unusable, in two distinct ways.

Solid height. Compress a spring far enough and the coils touch; it stops being a spring and becomes a steel tube. Solid length is \( L_s = d\,N_t \) with \( N_t \) the total coil count. Good practice is that a spring must survive being closed solid without yielding, because sooner or later something will close it — an overtravel, a misassembly, a maintenance hand. The worked spring reaches 564 MPa at solid against an 814 MPa allowable, a margin of 1.44: it takes the abuse and recovers.

Buckling. A compression spring is a slender column and will buckle sideways if it is too long for its diameter. The criterion depends on how the ends are held: a spring squared and ground at both ends against flat parallel surfaces is stable while \( L_0 < 2.63D/\alpha \) with \( \alpha=0.5 \), and one end free to pivot takes \( \alpha \) to 0.707 and the allowance down with it. The worked spring at \( L_0=90 \) against a limit of 158 mm has room; a long, slender relief-valve spring frequently does not, which is why such springs so often run inside a guide bore or over a rod.

§4 · Springs under fluctuating load

A valve spring is a fatigue component by definition, and springs are unusual in one respect: they are almost never fully reversed. A compression spring is installed with preload and cycles between two positive forces, so the mean stress is large and the amplitude comparatively small — which is exactly the situation Lesson 4's constant-life diagram was built for, transposed into shear.

Compute \( \tau_a \) and \( \tau_m \) from the force amplitude and mean, then apply Goodman with torsional strengths: \( \tau_a/S_{se} + \tau_m/S_{su} = 1/n \). For the worked spring cycling between 100 and 250 N, that gives \( \tau_a=107 \) and \( \tau_m=250\ \mathrm{MPa} \), and a margin of 1.81 — acceptable but not generous, which is honest for a spring working that hard.

One design lever is specific to springs. Shot peening the wire leaves a compressive residual stress in exactly the inner-fibre surface where cracks start, and it routinely raises the torsional endurance limit by 20% or more. For a highly cycled spring it is usually the cheapest life available — the same reasoning as grinding a shaft fillet in Lesson 3, applied to a surface that is otherwise impossible to improve.

Closing. Torsion in a wound bar, with the Wahl factor putting the peak on the inside. Rate goes as \( d^4 \), so wire size is the design. Then check solid height and buckling, which stress never covers, and peen anything that cycles.
