quiz.q:
Rate and stress at the working point

Problem. A helical compression spring has wire diameter \( d=4\ \mathrm{mm} \), mean coil diameter \( D=30\ \mathrm{mm} \), 10 active coils, and \( G=79.3\ \mathrm{GPa} \). It works at 20 mm deflection. The allowable shear stress is \( S_{sy}=814\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Find: the spring index, the Wahl factor, the rate, the working force, the stress and the factor of safety.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( C = 30/4 = 7.5 \). (2) \( K_W = \frac{4(7.5)-1}{4(7.5)-4}+\frac{0.615}{7.5} = \frac{29}{26}+0.082 = 1.197 \). (3) \( k = \frac{(79.3\times10^9)(0.004)^4}{8(0.030)^3(10)} = \frac{20.30}{2.16\times10^{-3}} = 9399\ \mathrm{N/m} = 9.40\ \mathrm{N/mm} \). (4) \( F = k\delta = 9.40(20) = 188\ \mathrm{N} \). (5) \( \tau = 1.197\frac{8(188)(0.030)}{\pi(0.004)^3} = 1.197(224.4) = 268.7\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (6) \( n = 814/268.7 = 3.03 \).

Answer: \( C=7.5 \), \( K_W=1.197 \), \( k=9.40\ \mathrm{N/mm} \), \( F=188\ \mathrm{N} \), \( \tau=269\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( n=3.03 \). Sanity check: the uncorrected torsion formula alone would have given 224 MPa and reported \( n=3.63 \) — 20% optimistic, and optimistic exactly at the inner fibre where the spring actually breaks. \( C=7.5 \) sits mid-range, so this spring is comfortable to wind as well as to load.

quiz.q:
Will it survive being closed solid?

Problem. The same spring is squared and ground, so total coils \( N_t = N_a+2 \), and its free length is 90 mm. Find: the solid length, the deflection and force at solid, the stress there, and the factor of safety against the 814 MPa allowable.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( N_t = 10+2 = 12 \), so \( L_s = dN_t = 4(12) = 48\ \mathrm{mm} \). (2) Deflection to solid: \( 90-48 = 42\ \mathrm{mm} \). (3) \( F = 9.40(42) = 394.7\ \mathrm{N} \). (4) Stress scales linearly with force: \( \tau = 268.7\times(394.7/188) = 564.2\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (5) \( n = 814/564.2 = 1.44 \).

Answer: \( L_s=48\ \mathrm{mm} \), 42 mm to solid at 395 N, \( \tau=564\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( n=1.44 \) — it survives closure. Sanity check: the margin at solid is above 1, which is the design requirement, and the ratio \( 564/269 = 2.1 \) is exactly \( 42/20 \), confirming the linear scaling used in step 4. A spring that failed this check would take a permanent set the first time anything bottomed it out, and would then be a different spring — lower free length, lower installed force — without anyone having replaced a part.

quiz.q:
The spring as a fatigue component

Problem. The same spring cycles between 100 N and 250 N in service. Take the torsional endurance limit \( S_{se}=310\ \mathrm{MPa} \) and the torsional ultimate \( S_{su}=1212\ \mathrm{MPa} \). Find: the shear stress amplitude and mean, and the Goodman factor of safety.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( F_a=(250-100)/2 = 75\ \mathrm{N} \), \( F_m=(250+100)/2 = 175\ \mathrm{N} \). (2) Stress is proportional to force, and 188 N gave 268.7 MPa, so \( \tau_a = 268.7(75/188) = 107.2 \) and \( \tau_m = 268.7(175/188) = 250.1\ \mathrm{MPa} \). (3) Goodman: \( 107.2/310 + 250.1/1212 = 0.3458+0.2064 = 0.5522 \). (4) \( n = 1/0.5522 = 1.81 \).

Answer: \( \tau_a=107\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( \tau_m=250\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( n=1.81 \). Sanity check: the mean stress is more than twice the amplitude, which is the normal signature of a preloaded compression spring and the reason the mean-stress treatment of Lesson 4 cannot be skipped here. Note where the margin is being spent: the amplitude term contributes 0.35 of the 0.55 total, so shot peening — which acts on \( S_{se} \) — attacks the larger term and is the effective intervention.

quiz.q: The dominant internal action in the wire of a helical compression spring under axial load is
choices: bending
torsion
direct tension
buckling of the wire
quiz.solution: The axial force acts at the mean coil radius, so a section cut through the wire carries a torque \( T=FD/2 \); the spring is a torsion bar that has been wound into a helix. Direct transverse shear is present but secondary, and it is folded into the Wahl factor along with the curvature effect. Recognising the action as torsion is what lets the whole component be built from a formula already known from Strength of Materials.

quiz.q: The Wahl factor exceeds 1 because
choices: springs are made from work-hardened wire
coil curvature and direct shear both raise the stress on the inner fibre
the wire diameter is measured before coiling
the spring index is always greater than 4
quiz.solution: Two effects act in the same direction on the same side of the wire. The inside of the coil is on a shorter radius, so it takes more than its share of the twist, and the direct transverse shear adds to the torsional shear there rather than opposing it. The result is a peak on the inner fibre — 20% above plain torsion at \( C=7.5 \) — which is precisely where spring fractures initiate. Work hardening affects the material's strength, not the stress distribution.

quiz.q: A spring's wire diameter is increased from 4.0 mm to 4.5 mm with \( D \) and \( N_a \) unchanged. The rate increases by a factor of about
quiz.solution: Rate goes as \( d^4 \), so the factor is \( (4.5/4.0)^4 = 1.60 \). The 1.13 answer is the diameter ratio itself and 1.27 its square — both badly understate how sharply a spring responds to wire size. This sensitivity cuts both ways and is the single most important practical fact about springs: it makes wire diameter a powerful design lever and makes an approximate substitution a genuine hazard.

quiz.q: Good practice requires a compression spring to withstand being compressed to its solid length without yielding because
choices: springs are always used at solid height
overtravel, misassembly or maintenance will eventually close it, and a spring that takes a set becomes a different spring
solid height is where the rate is measured
the Wahl factor only applies at solid height
quiz.solution: Springs are not designed to work solid, but over a service life something will close one — an overtravelling mechanism, an assembly error, a hand during maintenance. If that yields the wire the spring takes a permanent set, and it returns to service with a shorter free length and a lower installed force while looking entirely normal. That is a silent change to a machine's calibration, which is why the solid check is a standard requirement rather than a refinement.

quiz.q: A compression spring with \( D = 30\ \mathrm{mm} \) is squared and ground on flat parallel surfaces (\( \alpha = 0.5 \)). It is stable against buckling while its free length is less than about
choices: \( 79\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 158\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 112\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 40\ \mathrm{mm} \)
quiz.solution: \( L_0 < 2.63D/\alpha = 2.63(30)/0.5 = 158\ \mathrm{mm} \). The 112 mm figure is the answer for \( \alpha = 0.707 \), one end free to pivot — a real and much tighter limit, which is why end conditions must be identified before this check means anything. A spring that fails it does not lose strength; it bows sideways, rubs its bore, and delivers an unpredictable force, which is normally solved by running it over a rod or inside a guide.

quiz.q: Shot peening a spring's wire improves fatigue life primarily by
choices: increasing the wire diameter slightly
leaving a compressive residual stress in the inner-fibre surface where cracks start
raising the shear modulus \( G \)
reducing the spring index
quiz.solution: Peening plastically works the surface and leaves it in residual compression, which must be overcome before an applied tensile or shear cycle can open a crack. Applied to the inner fibre — the one location the Wahl factor identifies as critical and the one that cannot be improved by machining — it routinely buys 20% or more on the torsional endurance limit. It changes no dimension, no modulus, and no index; \( G \) is a material constant that no surface treatment alters.

quiz.q: A relief-valve spring is replaced by one identical in free length and coil diameter but wound from 3.5 mm wire instead of 4.0 mm. The valve will
choices: lift at the same pressure, since the geometry matches
lift early, because the rate falls by about 41% and the installed force falls with it
lift late, because the softer spring compresses less
be unaffected until the spring reaches solid height
quiz.solution: Rate goes as \( d^4 \), so \( (3.5/4.0)^4 = 0.586 \) — a 41% loss. Installed at the same compression, the spring delivers 41% less seat load and the valve lifts well below its set pressure. Nothing about this is visible on inspection: free length and coil diameter match, and the half-millimetre of wire is easy to overlook. It is the reason a spring whose job is a set pressure should be identified by its measured rate and treated as a calibrated item.

quiz.q: Compared with a fully reversed load, the fatigue state of a typical installed compression spring is
choices: large mean stress with a comparatively small amplitude
zero mean stress with a large amplitude
identical, since springs always return to free length
impossible to assess with a Goodman construction
quiz.solution: A compression spring is installed with preload and cycles between two positive forces, so it never sees a reversal — the worked spring runs at 250 MPa mean against only 107 MPa amplitude. That is exactly the regime Lesson 4's constant-life diagram addresses, transposed into shear with \( S_{se} \) and \( S_{su} \). Far from being inapplicable, Goodman is the standard tool here, and ignoring the mean stress would badly overstate the margin.

9.kuwait: Applied case — the relief spring that was replaced with a near-enough one. A pressure relief valve begins lifting early and chattering. Records show the spring was replaced during a routine overhaul with a part from stores that measured correctly on free length and coil diameter and looked identical. Its wire measured 3.5 mm against the original 4.0. Because rate goes as \( d^4 \), that half-millimetre took the spring from 9.40 to 5.51 N/mm — 41% softer — so the same installed compression produced 41% less seat load and the valve lifted well below its set pressure. Chattering followed for a related reason: with a softer spring the valve's own dynamics sit closer to the flow's, so the disc oscillates rather than lifting cleanly. Nothing was mismeasured and nothing was worn. The fault was treating wire diameter as a dimension to be matched approximately, when it is the single most sensitive parameter in the component. Two practices follow: a spring is identified by its rate, verified on a tester, not by its appearance; and any spring whose function is a set pressure or a set force should be treated as a calibrated item, not a consumable.
9.recap:
• A helical spring works in torsion: the axial force acts at the mean coil radius, so \( T=FD/2 \).
  • The Wahl factor \( K_W \) collects coil curvature and direct shear, putting peak stress on the inner fibre — 1.197 at \( C=7.5 \), and that is where springs fail.
  • Spring index \( C=D/d \) should sit between about 4 and 12; below 4 the coil is hard to wind and \( K_W \) climbs steeply.
  • Rate \( k=Gd^4/(8D^3N_a) \) — the fourth power means a 12% thinner wire loses 41% of the rate. Wire diameter is the design, not a tolerance.
  • Check solid height \( L_s=dN_t \): a good spring survives being closed solid without yielding (here 564 MPa against 814, \( n=1.44 \)).
  • Check buckling: stable while \( L_0<2.63D/\alpha \), with \( \alpha \) set by the end conditions.
  • Springs cycle between two positive forces, so fatigue is a large-mean, small-amplitude Goodman problem in shear.
  • Shot peening puts compression into the inner fibre where cracks start and typically buys 20% or more on endurance — usually the cheapest life available.

10.lecture:
§1 · The inclined plane, wrapped

Unwrap one turn of a screw thread and it is a right triangle: base \( \pi d_m \), height the lead \( l \), and the thread's helix as the hypotenuse. Raising a load on a screw is therefore the classic problem of pushing a block up an incline against friction, and the torque follows from resolving forces on that plane. The lead angle is what the triangle defines: \( \tan\lambda = l/\pi d_m \).

Note the distinction between lead and pitch, which is the most common early error. Pitch is the distance between adjacent threads; lead is the axial travel per revolution. They are equal only for a single-start thread. A double-start thread of the same pitch has twice the lead, and therefore twice the travel per turn, a larger lead angle, and — as the diagram shows — meaningfully better efficiency.

§2 · Torque to raise and to lower

Resolving on the inclined plane with a thread half-angle \( \alpha \) gives the two working equations. The thread angle enters through \( \sec\alpha \) because a V-form or Acme thread wedges the flanks together, increasing the normal force and therefore the friction — a square thread, with \( \alpha = 0 \), is the most efficient form and the hardest to make.

Key relation — power screw torque

\[ T_R=\frac{Fd_m}{2}\left[\frac{l+\pi\mu d_m\sec\alpha}{\pi d_m-\mu l\sec\alpha}\right], \qquad T_L=\frac{Fd_m}{2}\left[\frac{\pi\mu d_m\sec\alpha-l}{\pi d_m+\mu l\sec\alpha}\right] \]

The two differ only in signs — friction opposes motion, so it adds when raising and subtracts when lowering. If \( T_L \) comes out positive, torque is needed to lower the load and the screw is self-locking.

§3 · Self-locking, and what it costs

A screw is self-locking when the load cannot drive it backwards — release the handle and the jack stays up. Setting \( T_L>0 \) and simplifying gives a condition that involves no load, no diameter and no torque, only geometry and friction:

Key relation — self-locking condition

\[ \mu > \tan\lambda\cos\alpha \]

Independent of the load entirely. A self-locking screw holds a light load and a heavy one equally well — but the condition depends on \( \mu \), which is not a constant.

The worked screw needs \( \mu > 0.064 \) and has 0.15, a margin of 2.35. That margin is the thing to watch, because it is a margin on friction. Flooding a self-locking screw with the wrong lubricant, or letting a stem polish itself over years of service, moves the one number the safety property depends on. A screw that has been self-locking for a decade can stop being so without any visible change.

And the property is expensive. Because self-locking requires \( \tan\lambda \) below the friction coefficient, efficiency in that region is bounded — at the boundary itself it is 48.9%, and it falls away rapidly below. The worked screw runs at about 30%. Two-thirds of the work put into the handle is heating the threads. That is the price of a mechanism that holds its position with no brake, no ratchet and no power, and for a valve stem or a jack it is usually worth paying.

§4 · The collar, which is often the larger loss

A screw must react its axial load against something, and that thrust face — a collar, a thrust washer, sometimes a plain shoulder — has friction of its own. It contributes no useful work whatever, only torque:

Key relation — collar torque and overall efficiency

\[ T_c=\frac{F\mu_c d_c}{2}, \qquad e=\frac{Fl}{2\pi(T_R+T_c)} \]

Note that \( T_c \) scales with the collar diameter, not the screw's, and that it appears in the efficiency denominator without appearing in the numerator.

On the worked screw the collar contributes 67.5 N·m against the thread's 80.9 — 46% of the total torque — and takes overall efficiency from 29.5% down to 16.1%. This is the routine situation, not an extreme one, and it points at the cheapest available improvement: a rolling thrust bearing in place of a plain collar can cut \( \mu_c \) by an order of magnitude and very nearly double the efficiency of the whole assembly, without touching the screw at all. When a power screw runs hot or needs an unreasonable handle force, look at the thrust face before redesigning the thread.

Closing. A screw is an inclined plane, so friction sets everything. Self-locking is a geometry-and-friction condition that caps efficiency below 50% and depends on a coefficient that drifts. And check the collar — it is frequently the bigger half of the torque.
10.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Friction on an inclined plane (Statics L5) — the model the whole screw analysis is built from.
  • Coefficient of friction (Statics) — including that it is an empirical band, not a material constant.
  • Torque, work and efficiency (Physics I) — work in per revolution is \( 2\pi T \), work out is \( Fl \).
  • Thread geometry (Drawing & CAD L8) — pitch, lead, starts, and the Acme form.
  • Bearing pressure (Lesson 6) — the check on thread flank pressure that governs wear life.

Glossary

TermEquationWhen to use
Mean diameter\( d_m=d-p/2 \)The diameter every screw formula uses; not the nominal size.
Lead\( l = n_{starts}\times p \)Axial travel per revolution; equals pitch only for a single start.
Lead angle\( \tan\lambda=l/\pi d_m \)The unwrapped incline; sets both efficiency and self-locking.
Raising torque\( T_R=\frac{Fd_m}{2}\frac{l+\pi\mu d_m\sec\alpha}{\pi d_m-\mu l\sec\alpha} \)Lifting or clamping; friction adds.
Lowering torque\( T_L=\frac{Fd_m}{2}\frac{\pi\mu d_m\sec\alpha-l}{\pi d_m+\mu l\sec\alpha} \)Releasing; positive result means self-locking.
Self-locking\( \mu>\tan\lambda\cos\alpha \)Checking a screw holds its load unpowered; independent of load.
Collar torque\( T_c=F\mu_cd_c/2 \)Thrust-face loss; adds torque and no useful work.
Efficiency\( e=Fl/\big(2\pi(T_R+T_c)\big) \)Work out over work in per revolution; include the collar or the figure is fiction.

quiz.q:
Torque to raise a load

Problem. A single-start Acme power screw is 32 mm nominal with 6 mm pitch, so \( d_m = 29\ \mathrm{mm} \) and \( l = 6\ \mathrm{mm} \). The thread half-angle is \( \alpha = 14.5° \) (\( \sec\alpha = 1.0329 \)) and \( \mu = 0.15 \). It raises 25 kN. Find: the lead angle and the torque required at the thread.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( \tan\lambda = l/\pi d_m = 6/(\pi\times29) = 0.06586 \), so \( \lambda = 3.77° \). (2) Numerator: \( l+\pi\mu d_m\sec\alpha = 6 + \pi(0.15)(29)(1.0329) = 6+14.115 = 20.115\ \mathrm{mm} \). (3) Denominator: \( \pi d_m-\mu l\sec\alpha = 91.106-0.930 = 90.177\ \mathrm{mm} \). (4) \( T_R = \frac{25{,}000(0.029)}{2}\times\frac{20.115}{90.177} = 362.5\times0.22307 = 80.9\ \mathrm{N\,m} \).

Answer: \( \lambda = 3.77° \), \( T_R = 80.9\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). Sanity check: a frictionless screw would need only \( Fl/2\pi = 25{,}000(0.006)/2\pi = 23.9\ \mathrm{N\,m} \), so friction is consuming about 70% of the input — consistent with the 30% efficiency this screw turns out to have, and a useful independent check on the torque figure.

quiz.q:
Does it hold, and how much margin is there?

Problem. For the same screw, find: the torque required to lower the load, whether the screw is self-locking, the minimum friction coefficient that keeps it so, and the margin on \( \mu \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Numerator: \( \pi\mu d_m\sec\alpha - l = 14.115-6 = 8.115\ \mathrm{mm} \). (2) Denominator: \( \pi d_m+\mu l\sec\alpha = 91.106+0.930 = 92.036\ \mathrm{mm} \). (3) \( T_L = 362.5\times(8.115/92.036) = 32.0\ \mathrm{N\,m} \), positive — torque is needed to lower, so the screw is self-locking. (4) Condition: \( \mu > \tan\lambda\cos\alpha = 0.06586(0.96815) = 0.0638 \). (5) Margin: \( 0.15/0.0638 = 2.35 \).

Answer: \( T_L = 32.0\ \mathrm{N\,m} \); self-locking, needing \( \mu>0.064 \) against an actual 0.15 — a margin of 2.35. Sanity check: the self-locking criterion contains no load term, and indeed nothing in step 4 refers to the 25 kN — the screw would hold 2.5 kN or 250 kN equally. What it does depend on is \( \mu \), so the honest statement is that this screw is self-locking while its friction coefficient stays above 0.064, which is a maintenance condition rather than a permanent property.

quiz.q:
What the collar costs

Problem. The same screw reacts its 25 kN thrust through a plain collar of mean diameter 45 mm with \( \mu_c = 0.12 \). Find: the collar torque, the total raising torque, and the efficiency with and without the collar.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( T_c = F\mu_cd_c/2 = 25{,}000(0.12)(0.045)/2 = 67.5\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (2) Total: \( T = 80.9+67.5 = 148.4\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (3) Screw only: \( e = Fl/2\pi T_R = 25{,}000(0.006)/(2\pi\times80.9) = 150/508.1 = 29.5\% \). (4) With collar: \( e = 150/(2\pi\times148.4) = 150/932.2 = 16.1\% \).

Answer: \( T_c = 67.5\ \mathrm{N\,m} \), total 148.4 N·m; efficiency falls from 29.5% to 16.1%. Sanity check: the collar is 46% of the total torque while doing none of the work, which is why it nearly halves the efficiency. It is worth noticing that \( T_c \) depends on the collar diameter — at 45 mm against the screw's 29 mm mean, the thrust face has the longer moment arm. Replacing it with a rolling thrust bearing at \( \mu_c\approx0.01 \) would cut \( T_c \) to about 5.6 N·m and lift overall efficiency back to roughly 27.6%.

quiz.q: For a double-start thread of 6 mm pitch, the lead is
choices: \( 3\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 6\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 12\ \mathrm{mm} \)
\( 6\pi\ \mathrm{mm} \)
quiz.solution: Lead is axial travel per revolution, \( l = n_{starts}\times p = 2(6) = 12\ \mathrm{mm} \). Pitch — the distance between adjacent thread crests — stays at 6 mm; that is the distinction the two terms exist to make, and confusing them is the most common error in screw calculations. A double start doubles the lead angle's tangent, which raises efficiency substantially but moves the screw toward losing self-locking.

quiz.q: The self-locking condition \( \mu>\tan\lambda\cos\alpha \) contains no load term. This means
choices: heavier loads are more likely to back-drive the screw
a self-locking screw holds any load, but the property depends on a friction coefficient that can change in service
self-locking screws cannot be used above a certain load
the condition is only valid for small loads
quiz.solution: Load cancels out of the derivation entirely: it raises both the driving and the resisting effect in the same proportion. So a self-locking screw holds 2 kN and 200 kN alike. What the condition does depend on is \( \mu \), an empirical quantity that shifts with lubricant, surface finish and wear — which is why a mechanism can lose self-locking years after installation without any dimension having changed.

quiz.q: The maximum efficiency achievable by a self-locking power screw is
choices: about 30%
just under 50%
about 75%
unlimited, if well lubricated
quiz.solution: Self-locking requires \( \tan\lambda \) below the friction coefficient, and evaluating the efficiency expression right at that boundary gives 48.9% — approaching but never reaching 50%, for any \( \mu \). Better lubrication does not escape the trade-off: reducing \( \mu \) raises efficiency at a given lead angle but simultaneously lowers the lead angle at which self-locking is lost. Roughly 75% is the ceiling for a non-locking screw at a large lead angle.

quiz.q: Collar friction on a power screw
choices: contributes useful lifting work in proportion to \( \mu_c \)
adds torque without doing useful work, and so appears only in the efficiency denominator
can be neglected because the collar diameter is small
reduces the torque needed to raise the load
quiz.solution: The collar reacts thrust; it lifts nothing. So \( T_c \) adds to the input torque while the useful output \( Fl \) is unchanged, and efficiency falls. Nor is it small: collars are typically larger in diameter than the screw's mean diameter, and on the worked example the collar supplies 46% of the total torque. Neglecting it produces an efficiency figure roughly double the truth.

quiz.q: A square thread is more efficient than an Acme thread of the same size because
choices: it has a larger lead angle
its zero flank angle removes the \( \sec\alpha \) wedging factor that increases normal force and friction
it is made from harder material
it has more thread engagement
quiz.solution: A flank angle wedges the mating threads together, raising the normal force above the axial load by \( \sec\alpha \) and raising the friction force with it. A square thread has \( \alpha=0 \), so \( \sec\alpha=1 \) and that penalty disappears. Acme survives in general use anyway because the flank angle makes the thread far easier to cut and to fit with an adjustable split nut — an efficiency loss traded for manufacturability.

quiz.q: A screw raising 25 kN at 6 mm lead requires 80.9 N·m at the thread. The efficiency of the thread alone is closest to
quiz.solution: Work out per revolution is \( Fl = 25{,}000(0.006) = 150\ \mathrm{J} \); work in is \( 2\pi T_R = 2\pi(80.9) = 508\ \mathrm{J} \); the ratio is 29.5%. The 16% answer is the overall efficiency once the collar is included — correct for the assembly, but not for the thread alone, and the distinction is worth stating explicitly whenever an efficiency is quoted. Roughly 49% is the self-locking ceiling, not this screw's performance.

quiz.q: A valve stem that has been reliably self-locking for years begins to drift open after a change of stem lubricant. The most likely explanation is
choices: the thread has worn to a larger lead angle
the friction coefficient has fallen below \( \tan\lambda\cos\alpha \), so the screw can now back-drive
the load on the stem has increased
the collar has seized
quiz.solution: Self-locking depends on \( \mu \) exceeding a fixed geometric threshold — 0.064 for the worked screw. A lower-friction lubricant moves the one parameter the property rests on, and once \( \mu \) crosses that line the load can drive the stem backwards. Wear does not change the lead angle appreciably, and a higher load would not matter since the condition is load-independent. The general point is that changing a lubricant on a self-locking mechanism is a design change.

quiz.q: A power screw assembly runs hot and needs an excessive handle force. Of the following, the change most likely to give the largest improvement is
choices: increasing the screw's nominal diameter
replacing the plain thrust collar with a rolling thrust bearing
specifying a harder screw material
reducing the load's eccentricity
quiz.solution: The collar routinely supplies something like half the total torque while doing none of the useful work — 46% on this lesson's screw. Cutting \( \mu_c \) from 0.12 to roughly 0.01 with a rolling element takes the collar torque from 67.5 to about 5.6 N·m and nearly doubles the assembly's efficiency, without touching the thread. A larger screw diameter would actually increase both thread and collar torque, and hardness does not change friction in any dependable way.

10.kuwait: Applied case — the gate valve that would not stay shut. A large gate valve on a utility header is found partly open on a routine round, having been closed and signed off two days earlier. No one had touched it. The stem is an Acme screw that had been comfortably self-locking since installation, needing \( \mu>0.064 \) against a design value of 0.15. What changed was maintenance practice: a switch to a high-performance low-friction stem lubricant, applied generously at every service, had brought the running coefficient down over about two years. Once \( \mu \) approached 0.064 the line pressure acting on the disc could back-drive the stem, and vibration from a nearby pump did the rest. Nothing was worn, nothing was broken, and every dimension was in tolerance. The failure was in a parameter nobody owned — a friction coefficient that a lubricant decision had silently re-specified. Two lessons transfer. Self-locking is a property of the friction pair, not of the hardware, so a lubricant change on a self-locking mechanism is a design change and should be reviewed as one. And where the consequence of back-driving matters, the correct answer is not a friction margin at all but a positive mechanical lock — a handwheel lock, a gear operator, or a detent — that does not depend on a coefficient.
10.recap:
• A screw thread is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder: \( \tan\lambda=l/\pi d_m \), with \( d_m=d-p/2 \).
  • Lead is travel per revolution and equals pitch only for a single start — a double start doubles the lead and the efficiency benefit that comes with it.
  • Raising and lowering torques differ only in the sign of the friction terms; a positive \( T_L \) means the screw is self-locking.
  • Self-locking requires \( \mu>\tan\lambda\cos\alpha \) — independent of load, but dependent on a friction coefficient that can drift with lubricant and wear.
  • Self-locking caps efficiency: at the boundary it is 48.9%, and no self-locking screw exceeds 50%. The worked screw runs at 30% on the thread alone.
  • Thread angle enters through \( \sec\alpha \) — a square thread is the most efficient form and the hardest to manufacture.
  • Collar friction \( T_c=F\mu_cd_c/2 \) does no useful work. Here it is 46% of the total torque and drops overall efficiency from 29.5% to 16.1%.
  • A thrust bearing in place of a plain collar is usually the cheapest large improvement available.

11.lecture:
§1 · The duty statement comes first

An 11 kW motor drives a countershaft at 970 rpm through a V-belt onto a 250 mm pulley. The shaft runs in two bearings 300 mm apart with the pulley at midspan, and delivers its torque through a bolted flange coupling. The bearing pedestals are fillet-welded to a base plate. Size the shaft, the key, the coupling bolts and the pedestal welds.

Before any sizing, nail down the duty, because every number downstream inherits it. \( T = P/\omega = 11{,}000/101.6 = 108.3\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). That is the one quantity the whole assembly shares, and it is worth writing at the top of the calculation sheet where nobody can recompute it differently on page four.

§2 · Follow the load path

The discipline that makes an integrative problem tractable is to trace force and torque from where they enter to where they leave, and to size whatever they pass through on the way. Here the path is: belt → pulley → key → shaft → bearings → pedestals → welds → base plate, with torque branching off through the coupling.

The belt does two things at once, and forgetting the second is the classic error. It delivers torque through the tension difference: \( T_1-T_2 = T/r = 866\ \mathrm{N} \). But it also pulls on the shaft with the tension sum. At a typical V-belt ratio \( T_1/T_2 = 3 \), that gives \( T_2 = 433 \) and \( T_1 = 1300\ \mathrm{N} \), so the shaft carries a transverse pull of \( T_1+T_2 = 1733\ \mathrm{N} \) — twice the force that does the useful work. With the pulley at midspan the bearing reactions are 866 N each and the peak bending moment is \( 866 \times 0.150 = 130\ \mathrm{N\,m} \).

Note that the bending moment is larger than the torque. This is normal for a belt drive and it is why belt-driven shafts are almost always bending-governed.

§3 · Sizing, component by component

The shaft (Lesson 5). Reversed bending, steady torque, and a keyway at the pulley seat giving \( K_f=2.2 \), \( K_{fs}=1.8 \). DE-Goodman at \( n=2 \) returns \( d=34.0\ \mathrm{mm} \); specify 35 mm, at which the actual margin is 2.19.

The key (Lesson 6). A 10 × 8 mm key runs the full 55 mm hub. The tangential force is \( 2T/d = 6188\ \mathrm{N} \) and the bearing stress 28.1 MPa, giving a margin of 6.0. As always, the hub length set the key, not the torque.

The coupling bolts (Lesson 7). Four M10 grade 8.8 bolts on a 90 mm bolt circle, preloaded to \( 0.75A_tS_p = 26.1\ \mathrm{kN} \) each. The joint is friction-driven — the bolts are not in shear — so capacity is \( T=\mu n F_i r = 0.15(4)(26{,}100)(0.045) = 705\ \mathrm{N\,m} \), a margin of 6.5.

The pedestal welds (Lesson 8). The weld group is a 120 × 80 mm rectangle carrying 866 N of direct shear and a 130 N·m tipping moment. At unit throat the resultant is 9.28 N/mm, needing 0.064 mm of throat. The minimum 5 mm fillet the plate thickness demands gives a margin of 55.

§4 · Reading the answer, and writing it down

Line those four margins up — 2.2, 6.0, 6.5, 55 — and the design tells you something no individual calculation does. It lives entirely in the shaft. Every other component is governed by something that is not the load: the hub length, the smallest sensible bolt, the minimum fillet for the plate. If the duty rose 20% tomorrow, the shaft would need attention and nothing else would move.

That is worth knowing before anyone proposes an improvement. Heavier coupling bolts would buy nothing. A larger weld would buy nothing. Attention belongs on the shaft — and, per Lesson 5, the cheapest attention there is the keyway and the fillet radius, not more diameter.

The other half of the work is the documentation, and it is the half that gets skipped. A calculation package that another engineer can check needs the duty stated once and referenced everywhere; every assumption visible and attributed (\( K_f=2.2 \) for the keyway, \( T_1/T_2=3 \) for the belt, \( \mu=0.15 \) at the flange faces); the governing criterion named for each component; and the answer separated from the specification, because \( d=34.0\ \mathrm{mm} \) computed and 35 mm specified are two different facts and a reviewer needs both. Anything you would have to reconstruct from memory in a year is not documented.

Closing. One duty, one load path, four components, and a set of margins that says where the design actually is. The arithmetic here is Lessons 3 through 10 with nothing new added; what is new is the obligation to make it reviewable.
11.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Every preceding lesson in this course. Lesson 3 for \( S_e \), Lesson 4 for Goodman, Lesson 5 for the shaft, Lesson 6 for the key, Lesson 7 for the bolted flange, Lesson 8 for the welds. Nothing here is new theory.
  • Belt drive mechanics — that torque comes from \( T_1-T_2 \) while shaft load comes from \( T_1+T_2 \).
  • Beam reactions and bending moments (Statics) — locating the peak moment on a simply supported shaft.
  • Power, torque and speed (Physics I) — \( T=P/\omega \) with \( \omega \) in rad/s.

quiz.q:
From motor rating to bending moment

Problem. An 11 kW motor drives a countershaft at 970 rpm through a V-belt onto a 250 mm pulley with tension ratio \( T_1/T_2 = 3 \). The shaft runs in bearings 300 mm apart with the pulley at midspan. Find: the duty torque, the two belt tensions, the transverse shaft load, and the maximum bending moment.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( \omega = 970(2\pi)/60 = 101.6\ \mathrm{rad/s} \), so \( T = 11{,}000/101.6 = 108.3\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (2) \( T_1-T_2 = T/r = 108.3/0.125 = 866\ \mathrm{N} \). (3) With \( T_1=3T_2 \): \( 2T_2 = 866 \), so \( T_2 = 433 \) and \( T_1 = 1300\ \mathrm{N} \). (4) Transverse load \( T_1+T_2 = 1733\ \mathrm{N} \); each bearing reacts \( 866\ \mathrm{N} \). (5) \( M = 866(0.150) = 130.0\ \mathrm{N\,m} \).

Answer: \( T=108.3\ \mathrm{N\,m} \), \( T_1=1300 \), \( T_2=433\ \mathrm{N} \), shaft pull 1733 N, \( M=130.0\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). Sanity check: the transverse pull is exactly twice the driving force, which is what \( T_1/T_2=3 \) implies — \( (T_1+T_2)/(T_1-T_2) = 4/2 = 2 \). Note that the bending moment ends up larger than the torque. A designer who sized this shaft on torque alone would be ignoring the bigger of the two loads.

quiz.q:
The shaft, and what it is really made of

Problem. Size the shaft for \( M_a = 130.0\ \mathrm{N\,m} \) reversed and \( T_m = 108.3\ \mathrm{N\,m} \) steady, with \( S_e = 174 \), \( S_{ut} = 600\ \mathrm{MPa} \), \( K_f = 2.2 \), \( K_{fs} = 1.8 \), \( n = 2.0 \). Find: the required diameter and the actual margin if 35 mm is specified.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Amplitude term: \( 2K_fM_a/S_e = 2(2.2)(130.0)/174\times10^6 = 3.286\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3} \). (2) Mean term: \( \sqrt3K_{fs}T_m/S_{ut} = 1.732(1.8)(108.3)/600\times10^6 = 5.627\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^3} \). (3) \( d^3 = 10.186(3.849\times10^{-6}) = 3.920\times10^{-5} \), so \( d = 34.0\ \mathrm{mm} \). (4) At 35 mm: \( \sigma_a = 32(2.2)(130.0)/\pi(0.035)^3 = 67.9\ \mathrm{MPa} \) and the von Mises mean is 40.1 MPa, so \( n = 1/(67.9/174 + 40.1/600) = 2.19 \).

Answer: \( d = 34.0\ \mathrm{mm} \) computed, 35 mm specified, actual margin 2.19. Sanity check: the amplitude term is 5.8 times the mean term, confirming the shaft is bending-governed as the load figures predicted. Note the two distinct numbers worth recording: 34.0 mm is the calculation's answer and 35 mm is the specification, and a reviewer needs both to tell a rounded-up standard size from a padded one.

quiz.q:
The coupling that carries torque without shearing a bolt

Problem. The 108.3 N·m is transmitted through a flange coupling with four M10 grade 8.8 bolts (\( A_t = 58.0\ \mathrm{mm^2} \), \( S_p = 600\ \mathrm{MPa} \)) on a 90 mm bolt circle. The flange faces have \( \mu = 0.15 \) and the bolts are preloaded to 75% of proof. Find: the preload per bolt, the friction torque capacity, and the margin.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( F_i = 0.75(58.0\times10^{-6})(600\times10^6) = 26{,}100\ \mathrm{N} \) per bolt. (2) Friction acts at the bolt-circle radius \( r = 0.045\ \mathrm{m} \): \( T = \mu nF_ir = 0.15(4)(26{,}100)(0.045) = 705\ \mathrm{N\,m} \). (3) \( n = 705/108.3 = 6.5 \).

Answer: \( F_i = 26.1\ \mathrm{kN} \) per bolt, capacity 705 N·m, margin 6.5. Sanity check: the bolts never appear in shear in this calculation, and that is the design intent — a properly preloaded flange transmits torque by friction between the faces, with the bolts supplying clamp force only. Note the consequence for maintenance: the coupling's entire capacity is the preload, so a bolt tightened by feel rather than to specification removes a quarter of it.

quiz.q: A V-belt drive with \( T_1/T_2 = 3 \) delivers a driving force of 866 N. The transverse load it applies to the shaft is
quiz.solution: Torque comes from the tension difference, but the shaft is pulled by the tension sum. With \( T_1 = 3T_2 \) and \( T_1-T_2 = 866 \), we get \( T_2 = 433 \), \( T_1 = 1300 \), and \( T_1+T_2 = 1733\ \mathrm{N} \) — twice the driving force. Taking 866 N as the shaft load, the most common error here, would halve the bending moment and undersize the shaft. The 2599 N answer is \( 3T_2\times2 \) and has no physical meaning.

quiz.q: In this assembly the margins come out as shaft 2.2, key 6.0, bolts 6.5, welds 55. The correct reading is
choices: the design is over-engineered and everything should be reduced
the design is governed by the shaft; the other components are set by hub length, standard sizes and minimum fillets rather than by load
the average margin of about 17 describes the design
the weld calculation must contain an error
quiz.solution: Only the shaft was sized by the load. The key was made the length of the hub, the bolts are the smallest sensible size for a flange of that diameter, and the fillet is the minimum the plate thickness permits — so their margins are outcomes, not choices, and cannot be 'reduced' without changing something other than strength. Averaging margins is meaningless: a chain's strength is its weakest link, and any uprate or improvement must go to the shaft.

quiz.q: On a belt-driven countershaft, the bending moment frequently exceeds the torque. The design consequence is that
choices: torsion can be neglected entirely
the shaft is bending-governed, so the amplitude term dominates the fatigue equation
the key becomes the critical component
the belt tension ratio is irrelevant
quiz.solution: Bending on a rotating shaft is fully reversed, so it lands in the amplitude term over \( S_e \); steady torque lands in the much more forgiving mean term over \( S_{ut} \). With the moment already larger in magnitude, the amplitude term ends up 5.8 times the mean term here. Torsion is not negligible — it still sizes the key and the coupling — and the tension ratio matters a great deal, since it sets how much transverse load accompanies a given torque.

quiz.q: A flange coupling's bolts are described as carrying torque "by friction". This means
choices: the bolts are in double shear across the flange faces
preload clamps the faces together and friction between them transmits the torque; the bolts supply clamp force only
the bolts are loose and rely on the flange spigot
friction is a secondary effect added to bolt shear
quiz.solution: A properly preloaded flange transmits torque across the joint faces, exactly as Lesson 7 described for any preloaded joint — the bolts are tension members whose job is clamp force. Capacity is \( \mu nF_ir \), containing no bolt shear area at all. The maintenance implication is direct and often missed: the coupling's rating is the preload, so under-tightened bolts reduce torque capacity in proportion even though nothing looks loose.

quiz.q: The pedestal weld group needed a throat of 0.064 mm but a 5 mm fillet was specified. This means
choices: the weld calculation was unnecessary
the weld is governed by the minimum fillet size for the plate, and the calculation's value is in proving that the load is not governing
the weld is dangerously oversized and will distort the base plate
the load was underestimated
quiz.solution: Minimum fillet sizes exist for reasons unrelated to the applied load — heat input, fusion into thick plate, and practical control of the process. When the load requires far less, the correct outcome is to specify the minimum and record why. The calculation still earns its place: without it nobody knows whether the fillet is comfortable or marginal, and it is the evidence that a future duty increase has room here. This is the same pattern as the key in Lesson 6.

quiz.q: The duty on this assembly rises by 30%. Which component requires attention first?
choices: The coupling bolts, since they carry the torque
The shaft, whose margin falls from 2.19 to about 1.7
The pedestal welds, since they carry everything
None — every component had a margin above 2
quiz.solution: Uprating is governed by the smallest margin. The shaft at 2.19 drops to roughly 1.7, below the design basis, while the key, bolts and welds remain comfortable. The last option is the trap: it is true that every margin exceeded 2 at the original duty, but that says nothing about the new one. Note too that a belt drive's bending moment grows with the duty alongside its torque, so both terms of the shaft equation increase together.

quiz.q: The key on this 35 mm shaft carries a tangential force of 6188 N at a bearing stress of 28.1 MPa, against an allowable of 170 MPa. The right conclusion is
choices: the key is badly oversized and should be shortened
the key is set by the 55 mm hub length, and the resulting surplus is the transient and fuse capacity the joint needs
the key will fail before the shaft
the bearing stress should be compared against the shaft's strength, not the key's
quiz.solution: The margin of 6.0 is an outcome of making the key the full length of the hub, exactly as Lesson 6 described — no one chose it from the torque. That surplus is doing real work: it covers motor starting and jam transients that running torque never shows, while still leaving the key weaker than the shaft so an overload costs the cheap part. Shortening it to the load requirement would delete the transient capacity. The allowable belongs to the key's own material, since it is the key being crushed.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs in a calculation package a colleague can check a year later?
choices: Only the final specified sizes, to keep it readable
The duty stated once, every assumption attributed, the governing criterion named per component, and the computed answer kept distinct from the specified size
The most conservative result from each method tried
The software output, without hand calculations
quiz.solution: Reviewability means someone else can reach the same numbers without asking questions. That requires the shared duty in one place, visible assumptions — \( K_f=2.2 \), \( T_1/T_2=3 \), \( \mu=0.15 \) — since they are judgements another engineer may contest, the criterion each component was judged against, and both the computed and specified dimensions, because a rounded-up standard size and a padded one look identical on a drawing. Final sizes alone cannot be checked, and picking the most conservative of several methods after the fact selects the answer before the method.

11.kuwait: Applied case — the drive that was uprated on paper. A countershaft assembly of exactly this kind is asked to carry a 30% duty increase after a process change. The review is quick: the coupling bolts have a margin of 6.5, the key 6.0, the welds far more, so the assembly is declared adequate and the motor is changed. The shaft fails in fatigue through the pulley keyway inside a year. Nothing in the review was arithmetically wrong; the error was reading four margins as one number. Only the shaft was near its limit at 2.19, and a 30% duty rise took it to about 1.7 — below the design basis, while every other component remained comfortable and kept the summary looking healthy. Two habits would have caught it. First, uprating is governed by the smallest margin, not the average or the impression: the question "which component governs, and what does it become at the new duty?" has one answer, and it is the only one that matters. Second, a belt drive's bending moment rises with the duty as well as its torque, so both terms of the shaft equation grow together — a detail an average-based review never surfaces. The correct outcome was a larger shaft with a ground fillet and a relocated keyway, at a fraction of the eventual repair.
11.recap:
• State the duty once — \( T=P/\omega=108.3\ \mathrm{N\,m} \) — and reference it everywhere; every downstream number inherits it.
  • Trace the load path: belt → pulley → key → shaft → bearings → pedestals → welds, with torque branching through the coupling.
  • A belt drives on \( T_1-T_2 \) but loads the shaft with \( T_1+T_2 \) — here 866 N of useful force against a 1733 N transverse pull.
  • Bending (130 N·m) exceeds torque (108 N·m), so this shaft is bending-governed, as belt drives usually are.
  • Results: shaft 34.0 mm computed and 35 mm specified (\( n=2.19 \)); key \( n=6.0 \); friction-driven coupling bolts \( n=6.5 \); pedestal welds \( n=55 \).
  • The margins span 25×. The design lives in the shaft; everything else is set by hub length, standard bolt size or minimum fillet — so that is where any improvement or uprate must go.
  • Document so it can be reviewed: assumptions attributed, governing criterion named per component, and the computed answer kept distinct from the specified size.
